docs.abstract: Michael R. Bloomberg, the billionaire former mayor of New York City, has a new job: United Nations special envoy for cities and climate change.
docs.snippet: Michael R. Bloomberg, the billionaire former mayor of New York City, has a new job: United Nations special envoy for cities and climate change.
docs.lead_paragraph: Michael R. Bloomberg, the billionaire former mayor of New York City, has a new job: United Nations special envoy for cities and climate change. The United Nations secretary general’s office said Friday that Mr. Bloomberg would be responsible for nudging cities around the world to take steps to combat climate change, helping to “raise political will and mobilize action among cities” in the months before a climate summit meeting that is scheduled to take place in New York in September. The United Nations climate agenda has been entangled in arguments between rich and poor nations over who should more urgently take steps to reduce carbon emissions. As mayor, Mr. Bloomberg set a citywide goal to slash emissions by 30 percent by 2030. He tried to penalize taxi owners who did not use fuel-efficient hybrid cars, but the courts blocked that effort in 2011, calling it a de facto regulation of emissions standards — a power that, under existing laws, belongs to the federal government. Reuters first reported the news of Mr. Bloomberg’s appointment early on Friday. “I can’t think of a person better suited for this important new role,” Secretary of State John Kerry said in a statement.

headline.main: Bloomberg Picked to Be Climate Envoy

Directed by Chris Wedge, the movie is a hymn to nature rendered in phantasmagoric detail as refined as anything I’ve seen in a computer-animated family film. But as beautiful as it is, ‘Epic’ is fatally lacking in visceral momentum and dramatic edge.” Still, he added, “for what it’s worth, ‘Epic’ is on the side of the angels.”

docs.abstract: Dylan Farrow, Woody Allen’s adoptive daughter, speaks out about her experience.
docs.snippet: Dylan Farrow, Woody Allen’s adoptive daughter, speaks out about her experience.
docs.lead_paragraph: (A note from Nicholas Kristof: In 1993, accusations that Woody Allen had abused his adoptive daughter, Dylan Farrow, filled the headlines, part of a sensational story about the celebrity split between Allen and his girlfriend, Mia Farrow. This is a case that has been written about endlessly, but this is the first time that Dylan Farrow herself has written about it in public. It’s important to note that Woody Allen was never prosecuted in this case and has consistently denied wrongdoing; he deserves the presumption of innocence. So why publish an account of an old case on my blog? Partly because the Golden Globe lifetime achievement award to Allen ignited a debate about the propriety of the award. Partly because the root issue here isn’t celebrity but sex abuse. And partly because countless people on all sides have written passionately about these events, but we haven’t fully heard from the young woman who was at the heart of them. I’ve written a column about this, but it’s time for the world to hear Dylan’s story in her own words.)

headline.main: An Open Letter From Dylan Farrow

docs.lead_paragraph: Cheryl Boone Isaacs, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, defended that organization’s decision to rescind an Oscar nomination for the song “Alone Yet Not Alone,” from the film of same title, in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter on Saturday. The Academy had been criticized by some who said that it was biased because the song had come from a faith-based film. “This is not about the film,” Ms. Isaacs said. “We are adamant about keeping the integrity of our voting process.” She said that it was the appearance of undue influence by the song’s composer, Bruce Broughton, who emailed fellow members of the Academy’s music branch, prompting the decision to rescind the nomination. “Our purpose is to keep a level playing field and to keep it anonymous,” Ms. Isaacs said. “So when one person — in this case, Mr. Broughton — sends out an email driving the voting members to a specific song that’s his, it does break the rules.”

headline.main: Academy President Defends Ruling on Song

docs.lead_paragraph: As a kid in England, I watched a lot of television. There weren’t any books in our house,  not even the Bible. TV was therefore pretty important, omnipresent actually. Of course, most of what it delivered was garbage. But in 1973, the BBC aired an extraordinary documentary series called “The Ascent of Man,” hosted by one Dr. Jacob Bronowski in 13 hour-long episodes. Each episode was what he called an “essay” and involved some exotic and elaborate locations, but the presentation was never flashy and consisted mostly of Dr. Bronowski speaking directly and deliberately to the camera.

docs.abstract: The unusual greatness of a great actor.
docs.snippet: The unusual greatness of a great actor.
docs.lead_paragraph: Sometimes you don’t realize how much an actor has achieved until he’s unexpectedly gone. Reading the tributes to Philip Seymour Hoffman, dead this weekend at forty-six, I have the sense that his passing woke a lot of people up to his true significance, the full measure of his greatness, his distinctive place among his generation’s great performers. Not that he was underappreciated, of course — not with a Best Actor Oscar in his pocket and plenty of other critical garlands as well — but I wonder how many writers would have reached for his name, or at least reached for it quickly, if they had been asked to pick the best English-speaking actor of the last two decades just a week ago. Not as many, I suspect, as are reaching for the “greatest actor” label now, to describe his tragically-truncated career.

headline.main: Philip Seymour Hoffman, R.I.P.

docs.lead_paragraph: Robert Harris’s novel “An Officer and a Spy” has a point of high drama when the main character, Col. Georges Picquart, is ushered into a room full of atypical characters: people who will actually listen to him. For the first three-quarters of this book Picquart has operated quietly, trying to piece together the facts of the infamous Dreyfus affair, which culminated in the conviction, humiliation and banishment of Alfred Dreyfus, a French officer convicted on impossibly scanty evidence of being a German spy. docs.snippet: What it was like to make pictures of the notable actor, in photographers’ own words.
docs.lead_paragraph: Moved by the news of Philip Seymour Hoffman’s death, we immediately thought of these photographs, which the magazine had specially commissioned of the notable actor over the years.In the summer of 2002 the magazine asked Gregory Crewdson to create the pictures for the inaugural edition of a photo essay section of the magazine, “Portfolio.” For his setting, he chose an empty house in Rutland, Vt., that had caught his imagination, and for our part we decided to pair him with well-known actors, a departure for Crewdson, whose mysterious, haunting images until then had all featured anonymous subjects. Our hope was to bring a new twist to celebrity portraiture and produce some unusual images. One of the actors cast for the “Dream House” portfolio was Philip Seymour Hoffman. He agreed to go up to Rutland on a Sunday in August. I remember thinking, as we were driving to meet up with him at our rendezvous in a shopping center parking lot, How will we know which car he is in? But there in the big empty lot, in one lone car smack in the middle of it, was a man reading The New York Times. Philip Seymour Hoffman knew how to make an entrance.

headline.main: Three Views of Philip Seymour Hoffman

docs.abstract: The disruption of Sunday’s election by protesters could imperil the country and its economy.
docs.snippet: The disruption of Sunday’s election by protesters could imperil the country and its economy.
docs.lead_paragraph: These are dark days in Thailand, where an election on Sunday was disrupted by protesters whose demands for a suspension of democracy could lead to greater chaos. The country’s constitutional monarchy has faced coups and street protests in the past, but it has been a model of relative stability and development in Southeast Asia, a region known for its autocratic and brutal governments. As an American treaty ally, Thailand has been critically important in helping to reduce regional tensions and provided balance to the growing military assertiveness of China by championing trade and economic integration partly through the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. On Sunday, protesters disrupted the vote by blocking the distribution of ballot boxes to polling places in about 11 percent of the country’s electoral districts. Because Thailand’s Constitution requires that 95 percent of parliamentary seats be filled before a new government can be formed, the disruption means the country will remain in limbo for months as election authorities try to conduct elections in those districts where protesters prevented a vote from taking place. A gun battle between protesters and government supporters left seven people injured on Saturday, a day before the elections.

headline.main: Democracy in Thailand, Interrupted

docs.lead_paragraph: 10 P.M. (Starz Cinema) RUST AND BONE (2012) Ali (Matthias Schoenaerts), a former prizefighter fleeing with his young son (Armand Verdure) from a bad situation, arrives in Antibes, on the Côte d’Azur. At a club where he works as a bouncer, he meets Stephanie (Marion Cotillard, above, with Mr. Schoenaerts), a trainer for a Sea World-like amusement park. Then she loses her legs in an accident with a killer whale and calls him, thinking he might help rouse her from her despair. “A plot summary of ‘Rust and Bone’ might suggest a maudlin, therapeutic fable of healing, and in many ways — or, let’s say, in hindsight — the movie is just that,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times. “But its conventional, sentimental essence (which is overtly revealed only at the end) is effectively complicated, indeed almost undone, by the jagged textures of the filmmaking and the naturalistic intensity of the performances.” He added: “The removal of Ms. Cotillard’s legs — including in scenes in which she wears a bathing suit or nothing — is surely one of the most impressive special-effects feats of the year, and a reminder that digital cinema is not all about accessorizing wizards, monsters and superheroes. But the greater marvel is Ms. Cotillard herself, an actress of limitless bravery and supernatural poise, who is both beauty and beast. Mr. Schoenaerts is her perfect foil and complement, as large and coarse as she is small and delicate, and also as tender as she is tough.”

docs.snippet: What a British officer saw during his famous tour through the Civil War South.
docs.lead_paragraph: In early 1864, printers in New York and Mobile, Ala. began to publish one of the most unusual books of the Civil War: the diary of a British officer, Lt. Colonel Arthur Fremantle, who had spent three months observing the war, on both sides. Though he began his tour with a pro-Union bias on account of his opposition to slavery, Fremantle traveled extensively through the South. Entering through Mexico, he crossed the Rio Grande on April 7, 1863, and left New York to return to Britain 14 weeks later. His insights into the Confederacy, though at times myopic, especially on the question of slavery, offer one of the best single sources on life in the wartime South.

headline.main: Mr. Fremantle’s Adventure

docs.abstract: A new collection of photographs and stories chronicles a 500-mile bicycle ride along the mighty river — and the artisans found along the way.
docs.snippet: A new collection of photographs and stories chronicles a 500-mile bicycle ride along the mighty river — and the artisans found along the way.
docs.lead_paragraph: When Pete Seeger died last week, folk music lost one of its greatest pioneers, but so, too, did the Hudson Valley. Seeger had called the bucolic area just north of New York City home since the late ’40s, when he spent $1,700 for 17 acres in Beacon. It was from his house there that Seeger began, in the ’60s, his crusade to clean up the polluted Hudson River via his environmental nonprofit, the Hudson River Sloop Clearwater. Seeger was inspired artistically throughout his lifetime by the force of the mighty, meandering river, and it was Seeger that the British graphic designer Nick Hand initially had in mind when he decided, in the spring of 2012, to log about 550 miles biking through the region to interview and photograph members of its artisan community. The results are compiled in his new and lovely little book, “Conversations on the Hudson” (Princeton Architectural Press).

headline.main: Bookshelf | Portraits of the Hudson Valley’s Creative Community

Within Norway, the bicentenary is being celebrated with events throughout the year. In January, Queen Sonja visited the Norwegian Folk Museum to open, “1814-The Game for Denmark and Norway,” an exhibit that details the countries struggles for independence during the “Year of Miracles.” Visitors can also tour Eidsvoll House, which has been restored to look like as it might have when the constitution was signed there. The house opens Feb. 16, and tours run all year.

docs.lead_paragraph: It wasn’t so long ago that the gifted, indefatigably prolific theater composer Michael John LaChiusa was regarded as a theatrical wunderkind destined to be a future king of Broadway. It hasn’t turned out that way. Mr. LaChiusa, 51, has had his successes but no blockbusters. A major impediment has been his refusal (or inability) to write the kind of snugly packaged pop tunes that are Broadway’s bread and butter. To which I say, more power to him; the form needs composers as talented as Mr. LaChiusa, who have the courage to sacrifice commerciality and go their own way.

docs.snippet: With trimmer silhouettes and fancy fabrics like double-faced cashmere, the casual pull-on pant is fast becoming a wardrobe staple for the best-dressed set.
docs.lead_paragraph: Chalk it up to an increasingly casual workplace culture, the rise of the urban freelancer or the advent of the couch-to-dinner weekend wardrobe. Whatever the case, the old-school sweatpant, made modern with a slim cut and more refined fabrics, is now being heralded as the “new khaki.” Luxe versions of the stretch-waist pants are showing up on runways and in presentations in both Europe and New York, where the men’s shows continue this week. For his fall/winter 2014 collection, Michael Kors explained that he blended “New York City polish with the laid-back attitude of California,” and that he did away almost entirely with structured waistbands and belt loops. Made with double-faced cashmere or a more office-appropriate glen plaid, the newly refined track pant was the linchpin of Kors’s relaxed, elegant wardrobe. Meanwhile, Ralph Lauren introduced more sportswear styles under its Purple Label than ever before. A luxurious cashmere-knit jogging-style pant paired with a matching crew-neck sweater and trim topcoat stood in stark contrast to the nipped-waist suits that are at the heart of the tailored line, yet looked no less natty. And at Bottega Veneta, Tomas Maier paired belted coats, lightly tailored jackets and suede bombers with numerous iterations of the pull-on pant, from corduroy to cashmere, to signify his belief in this new trouser alternative.

headline.main: Three’s a Trend | Luxe Sweatpants

docs.snippet: The documentary “Afternoon of a Faun: Tanaquil Le Clercq” traces the life of a great ballerina who was paralyzed by polio at the height of her career.
docs.lead_paragraph: As you watch grainy kinescope footage of dancers in a mirrored studio executing a pas de deux in the documentary biography “Afternoon of a Faun: Tanaquil Le Clercq,” it is almost as though you are beholding mythological deities who have alighted briefly on the earth. Here today, gone tomorrow, they are like rare birds, seldom glimpsed, who remind us of the evanescence of all things, most of all physical beauty and the casual grace of youth. Therein lies a primal attraction of ballet: its evocation of the ecstatic moment is as fleeting as it is haunting.

docs.lead_paragraph: RAMALLAH, West Bank — For a while now I’ve wondered why there’s been no Third Intifada. That is, no third Palestinian uprising in the West Bank, the first of which helped to spur the Oslo peace process and the second of which — with more live ammunition from the Israeli side and suicide bombings from the Palestinian side — led to the breakdown of Oslo. You get many explanations from Palestinians: they’re too poor, too divided, too tired or that they realize these uprisings, in the end, did them more harm than good, especially the second. But being here, it’s obvious that a Third Intifada is underway. It’s the one that Israel always feared most — not an intifada with stones or suicide bombers, but one propelled by nonviolent resistance and economic boycott.

headline.main: The Third Intifada

docs.lead_paragraph: Eight Los Angeles police officers violated Police Department policy when they fired on two unarmed women in a pickup truck last February during the hunt for Christopher Dorner, the former Los Angeles police officer accused of killing four people, a civilian oversight board said Tuesday. Police Chief Charlie Beck will determine how to discipline the eight, who have been removed from field duty since the episode. Chief Beck said actions could range “from extensive retraining to termination.” The women were delivering newspapers when officers mistook their truck for Mr. Dorner’s vehicle, and fired more than 100 rounds. Last year the city agreed to pay them $4.2 million. Chief Beck said that although he sympathized with the officers, he could not excuse their decision to open fire. “This was a tragic cascade of circumstance that led to an inaccurate conclusion by the officers,” he said.

docs.abstract: The struggle for the future between a megalomaniacal prime minister, a cultish leader in the Poconos and thousands of citizens taking to the streets.
docs.snippet: The struggle for the future between a megalomaniacal prime minister, a cultish leader in the Poconos and thousands of citizens taking to the streets.
docs.lead_paragraph: It is still a marvel to behold Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s self-confidence, even after 11 years of his rule. In recent weeks, a new poster featuring Turkey’s prime minister has appeared throughout Istanbul, on highway billboards and mass transit. Wearing his usual dark suit, Erdogan looks to be in purposeful motion, like an action hero. Two large words in block letters, SAGLAM IRADE, Turkish for “Iron Will,” accompany him. Surely some of his supporters appreciate this evocation of 1930s-era masculinity, but for others, it must feel like an invasion of personal space. The enormous billboards intensify the claustrophobia that many Turks have felt for years: that Erdogan is everywhere, in every tree or open space sacrificed for a building, in every traffic jam, in every newspaper column and pro-government tweet and call to prayer. The poster, which a group of his supporters claims to have put up, begs to be defaced, and Turks have torn at it or covered it with new slogans: “Iron Fascist,” “Iron Corruption,” “Iron Enemy of the People.”

headline.main: Whose Turkey Is It?

The 32-year-old has pooled pieces by a number of behind-the-scenes talents, like the sought-after industrial designer Billy Cotton and the lighting expert Kacper Dolatowski, both of whose work had only been available to decorators seeking custom commissions. The handmade designs Ferrer displays, in a range of materials from brass to oak to plaster, feel classic yet current. “I don’t like to call it a showroom, which feels static,” Ferrer says. “It’s really more of a studio, an active place where artists refine, resolve and share their ideas.”

docs.snippet: The Pulitzer Prize-winning drama “Dinner With Friends” is being given a revival by the Roundabout Theater Company.
docs.lead_paragraph: Matchmaking is a dicey endeavor, and not simply because of potential guilt or awkwardness if the pairing doesn’t take. Donald Margulies explored more complex ramifications in his Pulitzer Prize-winning drama “Dinner With Friends,” which is being given a revival by the Roundabout Theater Company. In the play, one couple long ago helped two friends get together and the four were inseparable for years. But one marriage eventually shatters, and Mr. Margulies, instead of focusing on what went wrong, steers our attention to some collateral damage: the surviving couple’s contentment begins to fray in the aftermath.

headline.main: A Domino Theory for Marriage
headline.print_headline: A Domino Theory for Marriage

docs.abstract: I can still remember the first time I heard “Love Me Do.”

docs.lead_paragraph: I can still remember the first time I heard a Beatles song. It was the fall of 1964, my second year in an American school after my family moved back from overseas, and I was standing on the corner of 64th street and First Avenue with my friend Larry Campbell. I had a brand new, red, plastic transistor radio, and he tuned it to WABC AM and “Love Me Do” came on the air. The soundtrack of my life changed at that moment, with The Beatles becoming the recurring and dominant theme.

headline.main: The Beatles in the U.S., 50 Years On

docs.abstract: Pam Tanowitz Dance is at the Joyce Theater with a 50-minute double bill of world premieres, “Passagen” and “Heaven on One’s Head.”
docs.snippet: Pam Tanowitz Dance is at the Joyce Theater with a 50-minute double bill of world premieres, “Passagen” and “Heaven on One’s Head.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Some of the dance steps, phrases and constructions by the choreographer Pam Tanowitz are among the finest being made anywhere today. They feature memorable footwork, strikingly elegant and witty combinations of lower- and upper-body movement, and complex, subtle, fascinating uses of stage space. And yet she’s an eccentric. What’s notable — especially in the 50-minute double bill of world premieres that opened at the Joyce Theater on Tuesday — is that her eccentricity is intimately connected to orthodoxy. Much of her dance vocabulary is taken from ballet and from Merce Cunningham technique, both of which she employs in ways that should often impress devotees of either genre.

docs.abstract: One of the most sublime getaways in Europe just got even more transcendent.
docs.snippet: One of the most sublime getaways in Europe just got even more transcendent.
docs.lead_paragraph: In 1978, the English decorator Charlotte Scott decamped to the remote, semi-mountainous region of Andalusia. Fourteen years and four children later, she opened the doors at Trasierra, a 400-acre Anglo-pastoral guesthouse that she transformed from a crumbling 16th-century olive mill into a sanctuary of whitewashed courtyards, cushioned verandas and resplendent gardens. Starting in April, Scott’s 29-year-old daughter, Amber, who trained in Nepal and London as a yoga teacher and massage therapist, will be offering guests daily yoga classes. There will also be weekly retreats focused on meditation, hiking and massage sessions, combined with a delicious menu created by her sister Gioconda. Though Amber’s full-immersion programs happen in May and October, made-to-measure stays for parties of six or more are welcome year-round.

docs.abstract: Lino Brocka’s “Manila in the Claws of Light,” at the Museum of Modern Art, is a 1975 movie about the limits to life in the Philippines under the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos.
docs.snippet: Lino Brocka’s “Manila in the Claws of Light,” at the Museum of Modern Art, is a 1975 movie about the limits to life in the Philippines under the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos.
docs.lead_paragraph: Lino Brocka’s “Manila in the Claws of Light” begins with a whisper and ends with a howl. In between, there are grace notes, escalating horrors and the peripatetic journey of a country mouse, Julio (Rafael Roco Jr., later known as Bembol Roco), in the big city. It’s a story of struggle, survival, endurance and defeat that Brocka, perhaps the most celebrated of Filipino directors, filmed down and dirty in Manila when the Philippines was still in the grip of the dictator Ferdinand E. Marcos. Brocka, a political activist as well as a prolific filmmaker, died in a car accident in 1991 at 52, and is ready for rediscovery.

docs.lead_paragraph: LYNCHBURG, Va. — It was snowing hard on a recent afternoon, but Anne Spencer’s house glowed like a Vanessa Bell mural, more Bloomsbury than Old Virginia. Though Spencer, an iconoclastic poet and Harlem Renaissance figure, died in 1975, her singular house, with its purple, yellow and green rooms, its boldly patterned wallpapers and upholstery, its sheaves of newspaper clippings, photographs, N.A.A.C.P. ledgers, political fliers and her own copious writings that spill out of notebooks and climb the walls (Spencer was an enthusiastic wall-writer), is so vibrant that you would swear she was still living there.

Here, the imagery floats on plates and repeats on cups and bowls meant to be mixed and matched. Available at Bed Bath & Beyond, the line features five dinnerware patterns and four additional motifs on mugs and bowls only.

docs.lead_paragraph: Piet Boon, the Dutch architect and designer, recently opened a temporary studio at 404 Park Avenue South (28th Street), in a 1917 building that is being converted into 58 luxury apartments. Mr. Boon led the design team that outfitted the development, called Huys. He has furnished his atelier with his own creations, including Sam chairs upholstered in indigo fabric, shown with an oak Gerrit table. The studio also features other designers’ works, like Roderick Vos’s MaMa vase (on table), Frederik Molenschot’s brass numeral sculptures (on wall) and a Great JJ floor lamp by Centro Stile in Italy (shown in white). Though these items cannot be purchased on site, Mr. Boon’s staff can direct you to a dealer. The ground-floor space will be open until June, and then it will give way to a bank. Information: huys-nyc.com.

docs.abstract: A brief look at the harrowing and often hysterical week that kicks off every new fashion season.
docs.snippet: A brief look at the harrowing and often hysterical week that kicks off every new fashion season.
docs.lead_paragraph: For eight days in February and then again in September, more than 100,000 characters descend on New York City for the women’s fashion shows. Traffic grinds to a halt. Requests on Uber, the luxury car-service app, spike 40 percent. It’s harder to get a seat at certain restaurants, like Carbone or NoMad, than it is a front-row perch at Marc Jacobs. And there are enough crazed street-style peacocks clomping around and #NYFW selfies getting snapped to make the whole scene feel like some endless Kardashian nightmare. But it’s also serious business. The shows bring in an estimated $860 million for the city, more than the projected earnings of the U.S. Open, the New York City Marathon or the Super Bowl. Not bad for an event that began in 1941, when the International Ladies’ Garment Workers Union invited 30 journalists to attend a few designers’ showrooms. Here, a brief look into the harrowing and often hysterical week that kicks off every new fashion season.

headline.main: Temporary Insanity

docs.lead_paragraph: When I was young I lacked the patience and fine-motor skills to do much with Lego, but I spent a lot of time with friends whose bedrooms and basements bristled with elaborate, snapped-together spaceships and skyscrapers. Those intricate structures became, like just about everything else, stages for car crashes and action-figure duels. docs.snippet: Eyes appeared extra white thanks to an underline of an electric shade of blue.
docs.lead_paragraph: You couldn’t help but notice that flash of electric-blue liner peeking out from under models’ eyes at Creatures of the Wind this morning. But its reason for being there? Not entirely obvious. “It’s actually a lighting effect more than anything else,” revealed the makeup artist James Boehmer. “We pulled colors from the collection and eventually landed on this metallic blue since it gives the eyes a lit-from-within effect, and looks great on everyone.” To achieve the special-effects illusion, Boehmer traced a superfine streak of Nars Larger Than Life Long-Wear Eyeliner in Khao San Road on the waterline — that innermost part of the lower lid — so it would “catch the light,” he explained, and “shock the whites of the eyes so they stood out more.” The finished result was a bit ethereal, a bit punk and definitely pretty, even if that wasn’t the point.

docs.lead_paragraph: There is intrinsic power in escape stories; consider films like “Papillon” or “Escape From Alcatraz.” With “Riding the Midnight Express With Billy Hayes,” the writer Billy Hayes tells his own. It’s been presented before: in “Midnight Express,” his 1976 memoir about five years he spent imprisoned in Turkey for trying to smuggle hashish, and in the 1978 movie adaptation. Whether he’s nailing a bit of frayed rope to a wall or using a doormat, lumber and Kraft paper to build an Arp-like construction on the floor, he always creates work that is anti-monumental and abstract, as evidenced by “Looking for the Map,” at Pace Gallery on East 57th Street (Feb. 7 – March 15), which showcases 11 studies for his installation next October at Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall.

docs.lead_paragraph: Many people who worked with Hillary Rodham Clinton, from low-level aides in the State Department up to President Obama, “found themselves liking her more with each interaction, even if they had been worked over,” the authors of “H R C” write. They quote a member of Defense Secretary Robert M. Gates’s inner circle, who somewhat patronizingly describes it as traversing the “stages of Hillary”: “You know, you first dread the prospect of working with her, then you sort of begrudgingly begin to respect her, then you outright respect her and her incredible work ethic. You know, she’s inexhaustible, she’s tough-minded, and then you come to actually start to like her, and you just can’t believe it, but you actually like this person, and she’s charming and she’s funny and she’s interesting and she’s inquisitive and she’s engaging.”

docs.lead_paragraph: My wife and I are dear friends with a couple we cherish. At our son’s bar mitzvah last October, they approached my wife and told her they had forgotten their gift and would get it to us. When they came to dinner two weeks later, they had forgotten it again. We have seen them several times since, but the topic no longer comes up. We accept that they are never giving a gift; we love them anyway. Still, after every evening together, my wife points out the elephant in the room: “Still no gift.” How do we get past this, so it’s no longer on our minds? Should we say something?

docs.abstract: Claude Lanzmann’s latest film, “The Last of the Unjust,” focuses on Benjamin Murmelstein but is a more personal film than Mr. Lanzmann’s previous works.
docs.snippet: Claude Lanzmann’s latest film, “The Last of the Unjust,” focuses on Benjamin Murmelstein but is a more personal film than Mr. Lanzmann’s previous works.
docs.lead_paragraph: Perhaps the most haunting and enduring feature of “Shoah,” Claude Lanzmann’s nine-and-a-half-hour documentary — the closest thing to a definitive cinematic work on the Nazis’ mass murder of European Jews we are likely to have — is its dogged commitment to the present tense. Filmed mostly in the 1970s in some of the places where the killing was planned and carried out, “Shoah,” released in 1985, relies on face-to-face, after-the-fact testimony rather than archival footage or dramatic reconstruction. It is thus simultaneously about the imperative to remember and the inadequacy of memory. A masterpiece of historical detective work, the film is also a philosophical exploration of a gap that has only grown wider in the years since its release.

docs.lead_paragraph: The Québécois director Denis Côté throws a tight frame around his characters in “Vic + Flo Saw a Bear,” nearly boxing them in. That makes sense for this funny-eccentric, funny-scary story of two female ex-cons who having once been holed up together in prison are now holed up in a house in the deep woods. There’s a once-upon- a-time feel to both the location and the movie, which had its premiere at the 2013 Berlin International Film Festival, where it won an award. The title may sound like a children’s book and the bear may be metaphoric, but make no mistake: This is a story with surprisingly great, big teeth.

docs.snippet: The United Nations Relief and Works Agency, the body that provides assistance to Palestinian refugees, announced that a two-month strike by its employees in the West Bank had ended.
docs.lead_paragraph: The United Nations Relief and Works Agency, the body that provides assistance to Palestinian refugees, announced Thursday that a two-month strike by its 4,500 employees in the West Bank had ended. The strike, over pay and other issues, kept more than 50,000 children out of school, closed down free health services and raised tensions in the volatile refugee camps. The United Nations agency said in a statement that its director of operations in the West Bank and a representative of the area’s staff union had signed a document outlining measures to improve conditions for the staff, without elaborating. The statement praised the government of the Palestinian Authority for its mediation efforts and said the agency was “looking forward to the immediate resumption of all services.”

headline.main: West Bank: U.N. Staff Ends Strike

docs.abstract: President Giorgio Napolitano signed an emergency law to tackle environmental crimes and the damage produced by the illegal dumping or burning of waste.
docs.snippet: President Giorgio Napolitano signed an emergency law to tackle environmental crimes and the damage produced by the illegal dumping or burning of waste.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the first strong legislative response to the dumping crisis in the southern region of Campania, President Giorgio Napolitano signed an emergency law on Thursday to tackle environmental crimes and the damage produced by the illegal dumping or burning of waste. Under the new law, burning garbage without authorization is a crime punishable by up to five years in prison. In the vast area north of Naples where the Camorra mafia has buried toxic waste for decades, health and environmental authorities will have to carry out tests on the agricultural fields to measure the toxicity levels in the soil. Parliament allocated about $676 million for the cleanup, and police officers or soldiers will conduct antidumping patrols. The law includes measures to clean up the environmental damage produced by a steel plant in the southern city of Taranto.

headline.main: Italy: Toxic Waste Law Enacted

docs.abstract: In an effort to deter poachers and traffickers, France publicly destroyed a stock of about three tons of confiscated ivory from the tusks of African elephants on Thursday.
docs.snippet: In an effort to deter poachers and traffickers, France publicly destroyed a stock of about three tons of confiscated ivory from the tusks of African elephants on Thursday.
docs.lead_paragraph: In an effort to deter poachers and traffickers, France publicly destroyed a stock of about three tons of confiscated ivory from the tusks of African elephants on Thursday, making it the first European country to take such a step. The ivory was crushed in a large machine at a ceremony at the foot of the Eiffel Tower presided over by Environment Minister Philippe Martin. The impounded ivory included 698 elephant tusks that the police had confiscated and stockpiled since the 1990s. The operation was part of President François Hollande’s plan to “send a clear and precise message” against poachers, traffickers and buyers and “to show the French government’s solidarity to African countries,” the Environment Ministry said. The United States and China, ivory’s biggest market, have also destroyed seized ivory to help stem the illicit trade that endangers the survival of the elephants.

headline.main: France: Seized Ivory Destroyed

docs.lead_paragraph: The Food and Drug Administration updated safety requirements for producers of infant formula. The changes require companies to tighten their quality control procedures and reporting requirements. They also require that the companies meet so-called good manufacturing practices, which include testing for contamination from pathogens like salmonella. Most companies already meet those standards, but the rule will give the agency more control over enforcing them. The rule will also ensure that infant formula contains all federally required nutrients. The changes will be open to public comment for 45 days.

docs.lead_paragraph: 9 P.M. (Starz) BEFORE MIDNIGHT (2013) Nine years after rekindling a romance (“Before Sunset”) in Paris that began nine years before that (“Before Sunrise”) in Vienna, Celine (Julie Delpy) and Jesse (Ethan Hawke, above, with Ms. Delpy) are now in Greece, at the end of a summer vacation with their twin daughters (Jennifer and Charlotte Prior) and the son (Seamus Davey-Fitzpatrick) he left behind in Chicago. Jesse wonders if they could move from Paris to the United States to spend more time with his son. Celine sees his question as a demand to make it happen. And so they will fight about this — and the meaning of love, the nature of time and the difference between men and women — throughout the course of a day. “ ‘Before Sunrise,’ ‘Before Sunset’ and ‘Before Midnight’ are modest, charming movies that together add up to the great romantic epic of a generation defined, in the popular mind and our therapists’ offices, by hedged bets, easy ironies and perpetual confusion,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times of this trilogy from the director Richard Linklater. Celine and Jesse “can get on your nerves almost as much as they get on each other’s,” Mr. Scott added. “We have known them, and they have known each other, for a long time now, but we don’t know, from one moment to the next, what their future will be, or what it is that keeps them going. That kind of uncertainty, a scary fact of life, is something most movies avoid. We prefer the magical thinking of neat endings, tidy plots and clear character arcs. ‘Before Midnight’ is a wonderful paradox: a movie passionately committed to the ideal of imperfection that is itself very close to perfect.”

docs.lead_paragraph: David Glasner has a thoughtful post about wage stickiness, a favorite topic of mine. And he is partially right in suggesting that there has been a bit of a role reversal regarding the role of sticky wages in recessions: Keynes asserted that wage flexibility would not help, but Keynes’s self-proclaimed heirs ended up putting downward nominal wage rigidity at the core of their analysis. By the way, this didn’t start with the New Keynesians; way back in the 1940s Franco Modigliani had already taught us to think that everything depended on M/w, the ratio of the money supply to the wage rate.

docs.abstract: The major city of a complicated country, Yangon is hoping to become Southeast Asia’s next boomtown. What can you find during a visit in the meantime? Here’s a look.
docs.snippet: The major city of a complicated country, Yangon is hoping to become Southeast Asia’s next boomtown. What can you find during a visit in the meantime? Here’s a look.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s Myanmar’s moment, and the country’s major city, Yangon (formerly Rangoon), is hoping to become Southeast Asia’s next boomtown. Diplomatic missions, business delegations and tourists have filled Yangon’s hotels since the country’s military government began transferring power to civilian leaders in 2011. The spotlight continues this year as Myanmar, also known as Burma, takes on the chairmanship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. For now, though, as the road map for laws and reforms is being drawn, the city remains in a kind of urban time warp, still awaiting a much-needed capital infusion to fuel what it hopes to be its renaissance. Golden pagodas, colonial-era buildings, traditional shop houses and moldering jazz-age mansions form a low-rise fabric unique to Asia, the whole stitched together by tree-lined avenues swarming with buses and cars. While ethnic and religious tensions simmer along Myanmar’s borderlands, including in remote Rakhine State, where there have been recent outbreaks of religious violence, Yangon is far from these areas. Still, time will tell whether the city will reclaim its former status as a cosmopolitan capital.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Yangon, Myanmar

docs.lead_paragraph: Baz Luhrmann likes to say that his life is “a circus run like an army,” and to step into his boudoir is to begin to understand what he means. After noon on a Friday, the 51-year-old auteur is sitting up in bed, his lower half under the covers, silver hair and black T-shirt rumpled from sleep. His wife and frequent creative collaborator, Catherine Martin, known to everyone as C. M., lies curled beside him atop a flax-colored linen duvet. Four assistants occupy chairs around them, all holding laptops. Each of the young people who gather under Luhrmann’s big top has a fantastical back story, at least in his telling. One went to Eton and speaks perfect Chinese; another has a “grandpappy who created a little firm called the C.I.A.” All have areas of concentration — communications, for example, or “moving Baz through time and geography” — and all have been trained in “the Bazmark way,” which means that they carry portable tape recorders to capture his directives and strive always to anticipate his needs. Judging by their alert posture at this moment, something momentous is about to happen. The impish ringmaster is having a vision.

headline.main: Deep Inside Baz Luhrmann’s Creative Chaos

docs.snippet: The path to the summit of Croagh Patrick in County Mayo, Ireland.
docs.lead_paragraph: In A.D. 441, St. Patrick, Ireland’s patron saint, climbed the third-highest mountain in County Mayo and, according to legend, spent 40 days and nights fasting and praying at its summit. Modern pilgrims inspired by his example still flock to what is now known as Croagh Patrick. The Rev. Charlie McDonnell, a local priest, says that 50 years ago, most climbed the mountain on Reek Sunday, the last Sunday in July. But now, people visit the site every day. Some climb for spiritual reasons, barefoot and clutching rosary beads (Mass is celebrated frequently at the peak), others for their physical health. Even before St. Patrick’s famous ascent, the mountain was a pagan holy spot. “Patrick claimed the mountain for Christianity,” Father McDonnell says. “But we welcome everybody to the mountain. It is a sacred place.” Julie Bosman

docs.snippet: Throughout her 45-year reign, Elizabeth I’s private life was an urgent public concern.
docs.lead_paragraph: It was six yards square and extravagantly swathed in purple and gold, from its velvet headboard and valance to its voluminous damask curtains. The Virgin Queen took it with her when she moved from one royal residence to the next, chased by winter drafts and the inevitable buildup of noisome effluvia emanating from the rudimentary sanitation of her privy. As Anna Whitelock’s “The Queen’s Bed” proves, there is still a new and fascinating vantage from which to consider Elizabeth I. While most historians of the period dissect the body politic, Whitelock doesn’t waste time in the halls of Parliament. Instead, she hastens straight to the boudoir of the queen who chose celibacy as a means of wielding power.

docs.lead_paragraph: Visitors to the White House who seek out the well-known portraits of Jacqueline Kennedy and Nancy Reagan — ­eerie, El Greco-like elongations executed by Aaron Shikler — are sometimes surprised to have their attention arrested by Henriette Wyeth Hurd’s rendering of the far-less-chronicled Pat Nixon. The picture was created several years after the Nixons’ abrupt departure from Washington, and only for the sake of the subject’s daughters. The painted Mrs. Nixon seems stricken, ready to brim with tears. If the portrait could speak, it would most likely say what she herself did after the helicopter lifted off from the South Lawn on Aug. 9, 1974: “It’s so sad. It’s so sad.”

docs.snippet: The country-rock performer Eric Church, whose album “The Outsiders” comes out this week, casts himself as a renegade even as he racks up one success after another.
docs.lead_paragraph: What happens to the outlaw after he is embraced by the mainstream? It’s a recurring question in American culture, from “Huckleberry Finn” to Kurt Cobain. Eric Church’s fourth studio album, “The Outsiders,” is the follow-up to “Chief,” from 2011, which took him to No. 1 on the country charts and won the Country Music Association’s album of the year award. The new record, which EMI Nashville will release on Tuesday, represents a reaffirmation of his independent spirit in the face of an increasingly homogenized Nashville sound.

docs.lead_paragraph: OVER THE LAST 33 YEARS, E. Gordon Gee has presided over an astounding five universities — Ohio State, Vanderbilt, Brown, West Virginia (twice) and Colorado. But Dr. Gee, 70, has a habit of getting in trouble — comparing his job at Ohio State to running the Polish Army, calling the fathers at Notre Dame “holy on Sunday, but holy hell the rest of the week.” He has come under fire for his high compensation (he made nearly $2 million at Ohio State) and his high-flying expense account. (His response: If he’s not worth it, fire him.) Still, Dr. Gee, named Time magazine’s top college president in 2009, is a constant presence on state and national policy commissions. He is finishing a book on the politics of higher education, and after stepping down at Ohio State on July 1, he’s back in office — last month, he became interim president of West Virginia University, where he served as president in the 1980s.

docs.lead_paragraph: Photorealism was one of the major movements in American art of the early 1970s. A natural offshoot of Pop Art and heir to one-man movements like Edward Hopper, photorealist paintings depicted the postwar American landscape, highlighting Vietnam War pessimism and the plight of working-class people in the recession-era ’70s. The gritty realism of these painters mirrored the films of directors like Barbara Kopple, John Cassavetes or Robert Altman, or the minimalist fiction of Raymond Carver and Jayne Anne Phillips.

docs.lead_paragraph: In Sunday’s magazine, Adam Sternbergh riffs on so-called guilty pleasures. “How did these two concepts ever come to be married anyway?” he asks. “Aside from the obvious (sex), there are only three other arenas in life in which guilt and pleasure are habitually linked: gastronomy, religion and the arts. And while there are semi-plausible rationalizations for the first two (that cake was delicious, but I ate too much; I indulged in an act I’ve been taught to feel is wrong), for the life of me I’ve never been able to unravel how cultural guilt and cultural pleasure became so entwined.”

docs.lead_paragraph: You can always count on the Rag & Bone girl to make the call on what’s cool, beauty-wise. For fall, the answer is: loads of graphic eyeliner. “I was inspired by yé-yé girls from the ’60s, like Françoise Hardy,” the makeup artist Gucci Westman said of the “tomboy-ish” look she created backstage this afternoon. Her muse is “accessible and cool,” Westman continued, but has a “contemporary edge and toughness.” In the makeup chair, that translated into a modern cat-eye with a strong, geometric shape. The eyeliner “goes straight out, and doesn’t follow the lash line, which makes it slightly different,” Westman explained of her technique, which involved topping Revlon ColorStay Crème Gel Liner with Revlon ColorStay Liquid Eye Pen. To clean up the edges, Westman relied on an angled Q-Tip when necessary; she left the rest of the face relatively bare. “The eyeliner is meant to be your one trick,” she said. “This is not a high-maintenance girl.” Indeed, the British model Georgia May Jagger paid Westman the ultimate compliment by describing the finished look as “quite normal — it’s actually something I would wear out.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Liner Notes at Rag & Bone

docs.lead_paragraph: 8 P.M. (HBO) 42 (2013) Chadwick Boseman, above, portrays Jackie Robinson, a shortstop for the Kansas City Monarchs of the Negro leagues, a four-sport athlete at U.C.L.A. and an Army officer during World War II. Harrison Ford plays Branch Rickey, the president and general manager of the Brooklyn Dodgers who selected Robinson to become the first black major leaguer of the modern era. But when Rickey calls his new player “superhuman,” what he means is that Robinson will have to rise above ordinary temptations in the face of prejudice and hostility to become a flawless exemplar of his race. “While ‘42,’ Brian Helgeland’s new film about Robinson, gestures toward the complicated and painful history in which its subject was embroiled,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York York Times, “it is blunt, simple and sentimental, using time-tested methods to teach a clear and rousing lesson.” He continued, “In other hands — Spike Lee’s, let’s say, or even Clint Eastwood’s — ‘42’ might have taken a tougher, more contentious look at the breaking of Major League Baseball’s color barrier.” But Mr. Helgeland “has honorably sacrificed the chance to make a great movie in the interest of making one that is accessible and inspiring. Though not accurate in every particular, the movie mostly succeeds in respecting the facts of history and the personality of its hero, and in reminding audiences why he mattered.”

headline.main: What’s On Saturday

docs.lead_paragraph: ONE of my earliest memories is of sitting in an idling car with my mom and sister outside a convenience store in Virginia. Dad’s inside, buying cigarettes and scratch-off lottery tickets. Suddenly, a wild-eyed man appears at the driver-side window, yelling about white women and black men and how they don’t belong together. My mother goes feral, blocking his access to us. My father runs out, furious and swearing, before driving us away. I don’t remember what happened next, just a confusing and searing shame about the ugliness that the sight of my family could provoke.

docs.abstract: An increase would help 27.8 million people. It would also help balance power in the workplace.
docs.snippet: An increase would help 27.8 million people. It would also help balance power in the workplace.
docs.lead_paragraph: The political posturing over raising the minimum wage sometimes obscures the huge and growing number of low-wage workers it would affect. An estimated 27.8 million people would earn more money under the Democratic proposal to lift the hourly minimum from $7.25 today to $10.10 by 2016. And most of them do not fit the low-wage stereotype of a teenager with a summer job. docs.abstract: A single photograph of a woman’s legs may be titillating. But a cluster of 30 glamorous gams cut from the pages of glossy magazines is more than that.
docs.snippet: A single photograph of a woman’s legs may be titillating. But a cluster of 30 glamorous gams cut from the pages of glossy magazines is more than that.
docs.lead_paragraph: A single photograph of a woman’s legs may be titillating. But a cluster of 30 glamorous gams cut from the pages of glossy magazines is more than that. “Legs,” by the German artist Hans-Peter Feldmann, questions, with an erotomaniac’s attention to detail, advertising’s ravenous commodification of beauty. The 73-year-old’s work, an obsessive appropriation of everyday objects — from photographs of unmade beds to the front pages of 250 newspapers dated Sept. 12, 2001 — is in line with that of American conceptualists like Richard Prince and Dash Snow. And yet, he has trouble explaining his ideas: “When they asked the Austrian composer Bruckner what inspired his masterwork ‘Te Deum,’ he said it came to him while . . . eating a cheese sandwich.” Feldmann frankly loves sitting in a cafe and admiring the pretty passers-by, but says that the best legs he knows belong to Ursula, his wife of more than 40 years. “Is it sexist of me to focus so much on a woman’s legs?” he wonders. “I don’t know. Ask the great inventor in the sky.”

docs.abstract: The masculine hair at last night’s show was inspired by one of the designer’s own fashion sketches.
docs.snippet: The masculine hair at last night’s show was inspired by one of the designer’s own fashion sketches.
docs.lead_paragraph: “I wanted to do hair that was very drawn on, like an illustration,” the hairstylist Guido Palau said of the superslick and tight-to-the-head looks he created backstage at Alexander Wang last night. Fittingly, the inspiration turned out to be a fashion sketch the designer penned himself in advance of the show. To bring it all to life, Palau etched a deep side part with his comb and saturated strands in Redken Control Addict 28 High-Control Hairspray before wrapping them firmly around the head. “It’s like a very low sweep-over, like a man’s hair,” he remarked (otherwise known as the comb-over; who knew it could look so cool?). Palau then patted on a Redken Shine Flash 02 Glistening Mist for some sheen, and pulled strands into a slim ponytail, which was later tucked out of sight into the models’ clothing. To reinforce this idea of hair-as-fashion-illustration, he also “painted away” the part lines with makeup to prevent any skin from showing, and gave the models who closed the show — including Karlie Kloss, Jacquetta Wheeler and Joan Smalls — a blast of colored hair powder for an ultra-matte effect, like ink set to dry on paper.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Parting Ways at Alexander Wang

docs.lead_paragraph: Fox has canceled its version of the singing competition series “The X Factor” after three seasons. The announcement followed a statement by the program’s creator, Simon Cowell, who said that he would resume his hosting duties this year on the original British incarnation. “Last year, for a number of reasons, I had to make a decision to return to the U.K. version of ‘The X Factor’ in 2014,” Mr. Cowell said. “So for now, I’m back to the U.K., and I want to thank Fox for being an incredible partner, and I also want to thank everybody who has supported my shows.” “The X Factor” completed its third season in December, drawing 6.2 million total viewers for its finale. Before the series premiere in September 2011, Mr. Cowell said that if the show did not pull in 20 million viewers, it would have to be considered a failure. It fell well short of that, attracting 12.5 million at the start, and it never matched the ratings heights of “American Idol” (once the judging home of Mr. Cowell) on Fox or “The Voice” on NBC.

headline.main: Fox Cancels ‘The X Factor’ After Three Seasons

docs.lead_paragraph: Diahann Carroll has dropped out of the Broadway revival of Lorraine Hansberry’s 1959 drama “A Raisin in the Sun.” Ms. Carroll, 78, below, was cast for the role of Lena Younger opposite Denzel Washington as Walter Lee Younger, but she has decided to withdraw “due to the demands of the vigorous rehearsal schedule and the subsequent eight-performances-a-week playing schedule,” according to Philip Rinaldi, a spokesman for the production. LaTanya Richardson Jackson (“Joe Turner’s Come and Gone”) is to assume the role in her place. This was to be Ms. Carroll’s first role on Broadway in over 30 years. She last appeared in a production of John Pielmeier’s play “Agnes of God” in 1983. In 2004, Ms. Carroll, a breast cancer survivor, also had to drop out of a Kennedy Center production of Ernest Thompson’s “On Golden Pond” because of a herniated disk and severe muscle strain. “A Raisin in the Sun” is scheduled to begin previews on March 8 at the Ethel Barrymore Theater, with opening night set for April 3 for a 14-week run.

docs.lead_paragraph: Growing up involves successive acts of bravery. You must learn how to cross a street, pass examinations, take public transportation — things that so soon become standard fare that we forget their initial challenge. And so it is with dance. Child dancers regularly learn aspects of technique that are beyond the capacity of us nondancers. But in big theaters, it’s easy to take much for granted — whereas studio conditions bring us closer to the practical physics of ballet. On Saturday night, when the young dancers of American Ballet Theater’s Studio Company performed at the 92nd Street Y Buttenwieser Hall, their courage was evident — and admirable — in the opening ensemble adagio of the first item.

docs.abstract: A group of police officers became sudden celebrities by covering “Get Lucky,” Daft Punk’s Grammy Award-winning record of the year, shortly before the opening ceremony of the Olympics.
docs.snippet: A group of police officers became sudden celebrities by covering “Get Lucky,” Daft Punk’s Grammy Award-winning record of the year, shortly before the opening ceremony of the Olympics.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Olympics usually mint new and unlikely stars. Nearly always, they are athletes. But on Friday night, a group of mostly stern-looking police officers became sudden celebrities by covering “Get Lucky,” Daft Punk’s Grammy Award-winning record of the year shortly before the opening ceremony of the Winter Games from Sochi, Russia. The performance by the Ministry of Internal Affairs choir of “Get Lucky” went viral: It has been seen about 750,000 times since NBC posted it online. The choir’s reward: an appearance on Monday morning on NBC’s “Today.” The incongruity of the choir, dressed in evergreen uniforms accented by yellow braided cords, performing the slightly racy song (“She’s up all night for good fun/I’m up all night to get lucky”), doubtlessly accounts for its appeal. The two lead singers were the stars (a baritone joined them later); some others bobbed their heads but did not get funky, while others looked uncomfortable at their surreal dip into dance music. Rolling Stone labeled the police choir’s rendition “incredible” and noted “the officers’ hilarious ‘old, goofy man dancing at a wedding reception’ dance moves.” A spokeswoman for Daft Punk had no comment on the choir’s cover. The performance followed a studio version of the same number that was posted on YouTube in November. That performance, even more animated than Friday’s, has been viewed nearly 4.4 million times.

headline.main: ‘Get Lucky,’ Sochi Style

docs.abstract: The vaccine can protect against cancer-causing strains of the virus, which is transmitted by intimate contact.
docs.snippet: The vaccine can protect against cancer-causing strains of the virus, which is transmitted by intimate contact.
docs.lead_paragraph: Not enough children in the United States are being vaccinated against the cancer-causing human papillomavirus, or HPV, according to a report issued on Monday by the President’s Cancer Panel. The viruses, transmitted by intimate contact, cause cancers of the cervix, vagina, vulva, anus and penis and areas near the throat. Vaccines can protect against two strains that cause most of the cancers, and a series of three injections is recommended for boys and girls starting at age 11 to 12. But in 2012, only about a third of girls ages 13 to 15 and less than 7 percent of boys in the United States had received the shots. Vaccination rates are much higher in Australia (71.2 percent) and Britain (60.4 percent). Doctors and parents need better education, the report says, and it also urges that pharmacists be allowed to give the injections.

headline.main: Report Says Not Enough Children Get HPV Vaccine
headline.print_headline: Vaccinations Against HPV Lag in Children, Report Says

docs.abstract: Russian ballerinas inspired the designer’s collection, which was topped off with slightly messy yet prim updos.
docs.snippet: Russian ballerinas inspired the designer’s collection, which was topped off with slightly messy yet prim updos.
docs.lead_paragraph: With show venues spread far and wide this season, there’s a certain athleticism involved in leaping around the city. On Diane von Furstenberg’s runway in Tribeca yesterday, the relative endurance of the day fit in well with the designer’s theme. “The collection was inspired by Russian ballerinas,” the hairstylist Orlando Pita said backstage. So naturally hair was whisked up into a bun. But Pita noted an important distinction: “Diane wanted the models to look like they were in rehearsal, rather than in performance.” Conveying that sense of unfinished, dashed-off elegance came down to misting BioSilk Dry Clean Shampoo on fine hair for body or rubbing BioSilk Silk Gel Medium Hold on thicker strands for control, and piling everything up into a high ponytail. The length of the tail was then twisted and wrapped around the base, and slightly spread out with the fingers to create a wide, round shape secured with a cupful of bobby pins. But just when the bun began to look too stage-ready, Pita pulled this last step: “The trick is to put finishing spray on your brush and comb back the hair vertically,” he said, demonstrating the technique around the crown. “This makes it look like someone has taken her fingers and combed her hair up.” It lent a subtle rawness, which did seem quite en pointe.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Ballet Rehearsal Buns at Diane von Furstenberg

docs.lead_paragraph: At least 60 people were killed and dozens injured in Burundi after heavy rains caused flooding and landslides in the small, landlocked African country, a government spokesman, Willy Nyamitwe, said on Monday. Harimenshi Hermes, a spokesman for the police, said that thousands more had been displaced because of damage to their homes. “Many houses in the suburbs were destroyed by the rain,” said Beatrice Nibogora, an information officer for the United Nations in Burundi. “Many of the victims are children, and the houses collapsed on them.” The government said it would organize burials for the dead and treatment for the injured. Torrential rains began on Sunday night and continued into Monday morning, causing power failures and cutting off roadways around Burundi’s capital, Bujumbura. The city sits on the shore of Lake Tanganyika near the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo.

docs.abstract: The Hemingway Collection at the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum is giving researchers access to a newly digitized batch of the writer’s daily ephemera from his onetime Havana home.
docs.snippet: The Hemingway Collection at the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum is giving researchers access to a newly digitized batch of the writer’s daily ephemera from his onetime Havana home.
docs.lead_paragraph: BOSTON — Ernest Hemingway was a hoarder. His own prose style may have been spare and economical, but he was unable to part with the words, printed or written, of just about anyone else. According to his fourth wife, Mary, he was incapable of throwing away “anything but magazine wrappers and three-year old newspapers.” A trove of some 2,500 documents collected and preserved at Finca Vigía, Hemingway’s farm outside Havana, and now digitized and newly available at the Hemingway Collection in the John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum here, includes diaries, letters, lists, telegrams, insurance policies, bank statements, passports, tickets to bullfights and the Longchamp racecourse in Paris, a brochure from a swimming pool filter company, a page of his son Patrick’s homework and seemingly every Christmas card Hemingway ever received.

headline.main: A Mutable Feast

docs.abstract: Hairstylist Paul Hanlon pumped up the volume (and the staying power) with layers upon layers of styling products.
docs.snippet: Hairstylist Paul Hanlon pumped up the volume (and the staying power) with layers upon layers of styling products.
docs.lead_paragraph: Hairstyles captured in fashion photography look amazing — but those coifs need only hold up for a few shutter clicks. Backstage at 3.1 Phillip Lim this afternoon, hair pro Paul Hanlon whipped models’ manes into tousled, sporty-slick styles reminiscent of Bruce Weber’s “O Rio de Janeiro” book from the ’80s, but with a durability that would allow the ‘dos to withstand the rigors of the runway (and several hours’ worth of afterparties). “When you see those pictures, somebody’s gone in and done the hair, and it’s a moment. This is 3-D, the models are walking and moving, and you don’t want anything to fall out,” Hanlon explained. Perhaps that was his full-disclosure reason for applying what he admitted was an “excessive” amount of styling fixers: He first brushed through volumizing mousse for body, then massaged on a root booster to help form a pompadourish flip. Next he saturated strands, section by section, in Moroccanoil Treatment Light to create a wet, separated texture all over, and combed Moroccanoil Intense Curl Cream through on the front before pulling the hair tight on the sides and high on the top. To finish, Hanlon doused it all with hair spray. The maximalist approach went over well, creating a modern vibe that model Maggie Jablonski described as “punk, but artistic and beachy.” The only drawback: how to wash out all that product? Just follow Jablonski’s directive: “Stand and watch it melt away in the shower.”

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Sporty 3-D Hair at 3.1 Phillip Lim

docs.lead_paragraph: Thomas Rose could see the Union troops approaching from the east. After five days of torturous travel on foot, he was about to make good his escape from Richmond’s infamous Libby Prison. Awaiting the arrival of his comrades, he noticed three soldiers to his rear. Assuming they were a federal vanguard, he rose to greet them, only to find himself recaptured. After wrestling a musket from one of his captors and firing it into the air, Rose ran toward the approaching Yankees. A dozen rebel soldiers quickly knocked him to the ground and bound him for return to Richmond, ending the short-lived escape of one of the masterminds of the Civil War’s most celebrated prison break.

headline.main: The Great Civil War Escape

docs.lead_paragraph: The innocence of childhood, glimpsed through the hazy filter of nostalgia, imparted a wistful, weirdly beautiful element to the makeup at Rodarte this afternoon. Backstage, the makeup artist James Kaliardos described the inspiration as the time when “you sort of romanticize things like movies and fairytales that stick with you, and affect the way you see beauty.” The Rodarte princess, however, is all grown up and has a dark side to her as well. Providing that much-needed edge: a pair of iridescent lip colors done in rich shades of mauve and lavender. “Kate and Laura are so into makeup, and the subtle differences in color,” Kaliardos said about the Mulleavy sisters, noting that they spent hours deciding on the final palette. The models’ skin tones largely dictated which of the two shades they would wear, but the application technique was the same: Kaliardos lined the mouth with either Nars Velvet Lip Liner Pencil in El Agua (a deep rose, to be released in the fall) or Nars Eyeliner in Mambo, a reddish brown, and then filled in the lips with a corresponding hue (Nars Lipstick in Dominique Audacious and Deborah Audacious, respectively; both available in the fall). Lastly, he topped everything off with a custom blend of glitter — rose and gold mixed into a base of lipstick and gloss — packed on the mouth with a small makeup brush for precision. (Note to those at home: Surgical tape helps to catch any sparkle fallout on your skin).

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Fairytale Lips at Rodarte

docs.snippet: E.W. Gantt’s path from Confederate general to Confederate pariah led him to Brooklyn.
docs.lead_paragraph: Henry Ward Beecher, the best known minister in the United States, took the platform in his beloved Plymouth Church of the Pilgrims in Brooklyn sometime after 8 p. m. on Feb. 10, 1864. Under Beecher’s guidance the members of Plymouth Church stood as the most committed abolitionist flock in New York and even throughout the nation. On this night Beecher deferred to Brooklyn’s mayor, A. M. Wood, who introduced the evening’s speaker, E. W. Gantt, “late a General in the rebel army.” Gantt took the stage in the beautiful hall. Plymouth Church of the Pilgrims had occupied this building at the beginning of 1850 and while the exterior was not especially prepossessing, with its simple brick facade, the sanctuary looked very elegant. The hall, with a seating capacity of more than 2,500, boasted the largest pipe organ in the United States at the time. White pews trimmed in stained hardwood filled the floor and balcony, with the pews set in an oval, giving the space a theater-in-the-round sense rather than that of a cathedral or Puritan meeting house.

headline.main: A ‘Repentant Rebel’ Addresses New York Abolitionists

docs.lead_paragraph: A panel convened by the Food and Drug Administration concluded that naproxen, the active ingredient in Aleve, did not pose a lower risk of cardiovascular problems than ibuprofen and similar pain drugs. The panel voted 16 to 9 on Tuesday not to change warning labels on naproxen, a broadly used anti-inflammatory pain medication, to say that it is less risky. Naproxen, which is widely used to treat arthritis pain, had been found in some studies included in a large analysis published last year in The Lancet to carry a lower risk for heart problems than others in its class. A large clinical trial comparing a number of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, including naproxen and ibuprofen, is nearing completion, and some participants said they expected that the results would allow for more definitive conclusions on naproxen.

docs.abstract: A Texas-size tale of ambition, motherhood and political mythmaking.
docs.snippet: A Texas-size tale of ambition, motherhood and political mythmaking.
docs.lead_paragraph: One sunny Friday morning in late January, Wendy Davis took me on a two-hour tour of the life she led just a decade or so ago, back when she was a city councilwoman and the world knew nothing of her or the pink running shoes she wore during her epic filibuster, or her ambition to be elected this November as a Democratic governor in the deeply Republican state of Texas, or the way her parenting has become a point of debate in whether she’s a suitable candidate for that office. We were in Fort Worth, where Davis, who is a state senator, has lived for about 35 of her 50 years, most in utter obscurity. When she joined the City Council in 1999, she was only the third-most-prominent Wendy Davis in town (the other two were socialites), and to the extent that community leaders knew her at all, it was as the wife of Jeff Davis, an attorney and former city councilman, whose civic passions would spark her own. Once that fire was lit, everything would later change for her — for her marriage, for her city, for Texas and, who knows, perhaps even for a national Democratic Party in search of a post-Obama non-Hillary superstar.

headline.main: Can Wendy Davis Have It All?

docs.abstract: In Rebecca Behrens’s debut novel, the fictional child of a president is inspired by the diary of Theodore Roosevelt’s daughter Alice.
docs.snippet: In Rebecca Behrens’s debut novel, the fictional child of a president is inspired by the diary of Theodore Roosevelt’s daughter Alice.
docs.lead_paragraph: Audrey Rhodes is a pretty typical 13-year old in every respect but one: The home she returns to at the end of the school day is 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue. In Rebecca Behrens’s debut novel, “When Audrey Met Alice,” the perks that come with living in the White House (swimming pool, bowling alley, fresh-baked cookies on demand) fail to outweigh the loneliness and restrictions Audrey suffers in her role as “first daughter.” Her mother, the president, is distracted by matters of national importance. Her father, a medical researcher known as “the first gent,” is often away at his lab in Baltimore. Audrey’s ordinary teenage conundrums — how to make friends at a new school; how to act around a boy she likes — are amplified by the demands of presidential protocol and security: she can’t even choose her own clothes. It’s no wonder Audrey, who doesn’t mince words, says she sometimes feels “like punching a hole through one of my historic walls.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Three blog posts and a column should probably suffice to cover the debate over Obamacare and work incentives, but I don’t want to let the topic drop without first stepping back and talking about the actual health policy disagreement here. My column and posts last week criticized what struck me as a kind of insouciance from liberals about this issue, shading into a post-work utopianism that doesn’t wrestle with what, in practice, the decline of work is actually likely to mean for issues of class, mobility, and social equality. But it’s also important to recognize that for many liberal writers, the controlling assumption here is not anti-work or pro-work. It’s just pro-universal health care as a basic standard for a decent society, with the consequences taken as they come.

headline.main: Work and Health Insurance: Is There An Alternative?

docs.abstract: Michael Sam’s father offers an excellent example of how not to respond to a child’s surprising news — and a good opportunity to reflect on how you’d like to react.
docs.snippet: Michael Sam’s father offers an excellent example of how not to respond to a child’s surprising news — and a good opportunity to reflect on how you’d like to react.
docs.lead_paragraph: Maybe this is a good time to take a moment and consider what you would say if your child made an announcement that really surprised you — especially if it both surprised and disappointed you. It could be, “Mom, I’m not going to college, because I’m traveling the country with my punk rock band.” Or it could be, “Dad, I’m leaving the Joffrey Ballet.” It doesn’t matter — but what you say does. That first reaction stays with your child no matter how you eventually turn it around, whether it’s disappointment in his choice of spouse or disbelief over her career decision.

headline.main: How Not to React When a Child’s News Surprises You

docs.snippet: Members of the Metropolitan Opera’s young artist program joined with the Juilliard Orchestra, led by James Levine, to present “A Concert of Comic Operas.”
docs.lead_paragraph: James Levine was just 37 when, in 1980, he inaugurated what is now called the Metropolitan Opera’s Lindemann Young Artist Development Program. His desire to foster young talent has now taken him across the Lincoln Center plaza to the Juilliard School. On Tuesday night at the Peter Jay Sharp Theater, he conducted the opening performance of a program of comic scenes from works by Mozart, Berlioz and Donizetti along with “Mavra,” Stravinsky’s rarely heard one-act. This ambitious program, lasting three hours, was the fourth co-production between the Met’s young artist program and Juilliard Opera since the two institutions began a partnership in 2010.

docs.abstract: Peggy Orenstein’s reporting in the magazine last year led her to the conclusion that when it comes to mammograms, there is such a thing as too much screening.
docs.snippet: Peggy Orenstein’s reporting in the magazine last year led her to the conclusion that when it comes to mammograms, there is such a thing as too much screening.
docs.lead_paragraph: The front-page news today that mammograms don’t decrease the death rates from breast cancer — but do increase the likelihood of unnecessary treatment — reminded me that it’s worth going back to Peggy Orenstein’s cover story from last April. Even before the results of the newly published study, involving 90,000 women, were released, Orenstein’s reporting led her to the same conclusion: There is such a thing as too much screening. And she made a powerful argument that the Komen Foundation’s pink-ribbon “awareness” campaign is a big part of the problem. She also wrote insightfully about how difficult it is not to have a mammogram even if the science tells us that isn’t helpful.

headline.main: The Problem With Mammograms

docs.abstract: New nesting containers from Joseph Joseph take efficiency to a new level.
docs.snippet: New nesting containers from Joseph Joseph take efficiency to a new level.
docs.lead_paragraph: In 1999, Antony and Richard Joseph, twin industrial designers, were asked to update a part of their family’s 63-year-old British housewares business. Four years later, they created their own company, Joseph Joseph, which produces smartly functional items for the home like colorful stacking mixing bowls with integrated measuring cups. Their Nest containers, shown at the New York Now design show last week, tackle the problem of storage boxes that hog precious space when not in use. Whereas lids and bases often need to be stored separately, turning matchups into a problem, this design efficiently packs together bases and lids for up to six sizes of containers; color-coding makes the pairings foolproof. The containers are airtight and microwave-, freezer- and dishwasher-safe. A 12-piece set (6 containers, 6 lids) is $35, and an 8-piece set (4 containers, 4 lids) is $25. Information: 917-338-0900, or josephjoseph.com.

docs.abstract: The people were killed in unrest in Caracas on Wednesday, officials said, as thousands took to the streets of the capital in the largest antigovernment protest in months.

docs.lead_paragraph: At least two people were killed in unrest in Caracas on Wednesday, officials said, as thousands of people took to the streets of the capital in the largest antigovernment protest in months. The violence erupted after government opponents attended a peaceful march and rally called to protest the arrest of student demonstrators elsewhere in the country. Following the march, several hundred young protesters threw rocks at riot police officers and broke windows in a government building. One demonstrator was shot in the head and killed, and protesters blamed armed pro-government supporters. Later, President Nicolás Maduro said a community activist he had known for years had also been killed. Diosdado Cabello, the president of the National Assembly, said the man was killed by “fascists,” a term the government uses for its opponents. Mr. Maduro later said on television, “I alert the world: we are facing a planned coup d’état.” The protests in various cities in recent weeks have sprung from widespread discontent amid increasing economic problems, including high inflation.

headline.main: Venezuela: At Least Two People Are Killed in Protests
