(Starz Cinema) THE DIVING BELL AND THE BUTTERFLY (2007) Jean-Dominique Bauby, a 43-year-old French magazine editor and something of a playboy, had a stroke in 1995 that left him with a condition in which he retained vision, hearing and a functioning mind but was almost completely paralyzed. He told his story in a book that he dictated to an assistant by blinking. In this film from the artist Julian Schnabel, Bauby is played by Mathieu Amalric; Emmanuelle Seigner is Céline, the longtime partner he has recently left and the mother of his three children; and Marie-Josée Croze is the speech therapist who teaches him to use his left eyelid to communicate. “The phrase ‘triumph of the human spirit’ hovers over ‘The Diving Bell and the Butterfly,’ along with a swarm of other empty, uplifting clichés,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times. “But Mr. Schnabel and the screenwriter, Ronald Harwood, have other themes in mind” — among them, limitation, constraint and incarceration — Mr. Scott said. (Both men were nominated for Oscars.) “Their common subject, however, is freedom, the self-willed liberation of a difficult, defiant individual,” Mr. Scott wrote, adding that Mr. Schnabel demonstrated this with “imaginative freedom in every frame and sequence, dispensing with narrative and expository conventions in favor of a wild, intuitive honesty.”

docs.abstract: Adam Gopnik’s unconvincing portrait of contemporary faith.
docs.snippet: Adam Gopnik’s unconvincing portrait of contemporary faith.
docs.lead_paragraph: I expected to be pained by Adam Gopnik’s New Yorker essay on atheism and belief, but I didn’t expect to be quite so … puzzled by his depiction of contemporary belief. Gopnik clearly has sympathy for the religious side of the argument he’s describing — or at the very least he’s straining to be sympathetic. But given the premises he’s working from, that sympathy manifests itself in a peculiar and telling misreading of what theists actually believe.

docs.lead_paragraph: Sadler’s Ordinary, occupying a barnlike structure in out-of-the-way Marlborough, recently celebrated its 35th anniversary. Few marriages last that long, and the restaurant business is even more fickle than matrimony. Welcome to 1978!

docs.abstract: “Forrest Bess: Seeing Things Invisible,” at the Neuberger Museum of Art, dives deeply into this painter’s life and work.
docs.snippet: “Forrest Bess: Seeing Things Invisible,” at the Neuberger Museum of Art, dives deeply into this painter’s life and work.
docs.lead_paragraph: PURCHASE, N.Y. — The small but potent paintings of Forrest Bess respond to the art world’s “either-ors” with a resounding “and.” Without resorting to big stretches of canvas or brash gestures, they merge inner and outer worlds, abstraction and representation, and ideas of masculinity and femininity. To a market still intent on labeling “insiders” and “outsiders,” they offer the conundrum of an artist who showed at the Betty Parsons Gallery in New York in the 1950s, alongside Rothko and Pollock, but made his living as a bait fisherman in Bay City, Tex.

headline.main: An Artist’s Paintings, and His Complexities, on Display

docs.abstract: The festival Film Comment Selects includes 22 movies chosen by the editors of Film Comment magazine.
docs.snippet: The festival Film Comment Selects includes 22 movies chosen by the editors of Film Comment magazine.
docs.lead_paragraph: Moviegoers may be experiencing a moment of mathematical confusion. Are there too many movies or not enough? Could it be both? At this time of year, interesting new commercial releases slow to a trickle, as the Oscar pachyderms dominate the landscape, making room for a few smaller films and the usual genre offerings — action, rom-com, animation, whatever. Slim pickings for the discerning cinephile. At the same time, bulletins from Sundance and Berlin, and reports from the not-fully-charted wilderness of digital distribution, suggest a state of unmanageable abundance, a cornucopia of docs, foreign-language art and genre films, and post-mumblecore youthquakes. There is nothing to see, but so much that we’re missing.

docs.lead_paragraph: Alongside its reputation for gilded, Buddha-filled temples and treks to hill tribe villages, Chiang Mai in northern Thailand has in recent years attracted creative types seeking a chilled-out alternative to Bangkok, 350 miles away. Nowhere is this more evident than Nimmanhaemin Road, a thoroughfare west of the old city center anchored by Chiang Mai University and known as Nimman. The area’s tranquil side streets, called sois, are home to quirky coffee shops, design boutiques and galleries. These, combined with boutique hotels like Artel Nimman, where guests access the ground floor by a slide, make Nimman an appealing base from which to explore the city.

docs.snippet: Film Forum opens a weeklong run of Alain Resnais’s “Je T’Aime, Je T’Aime,” whose central character travels through time, reliving a relationship nonchronologically.
docs.lead_paragraph: Most stories begin once upon a time and, after the usual chronological tramp toward the inevitable and an occasional detour into the past or future, end happily ever after (or not). In “Je T’Aime, Je T’Aime,” a magnificent film from out of the past, the French director Alain Resnais takes dozens of interludes from one man’s life — images of everyday banality and commonplace delights, scenes of him at work and at play — and arranges them nonchronologically. One minute, Claude (Claude Rich) is emerging from a swim, the next he’s violently quarreling with a lover, and then he’s emerging from that exact same swim all over again, as if stuck in a loop.

headline.main: Fragmented Frames of the Love That Was, Taunting Yet Poignant

docs.snippet: “About Last Night,” a raucously entertaining remake, follows the difficulties faced by two couples, one sensitive and well behaved, the other outrageously naughty.
docs.lead_paragraph: It is now 40 years since the first performances of David Mamet’s “Sexual Perversity in Chicago” and almost 30 since the play was made into a movie, starring Rob Lowe and Demi Moore and directed by Edward Zwick, called “About Last Night ... .” Some things have changed (Mr. Mamet has evolved into a dyspeptic right-winger) and some have not (Mr. Lowe and Ms. Moore are still very good looking), but all in all, the thing holds up pretty well. Mr. Mamet’s title was always a bit of a misnomer — his jagged play is more interested in romantic confusion and emotional complication than in freaky bedroom matters — but his map of the crooked paths to heterosexual bliss remains useful and adaptable, even when softened and tidied up by Hollywood. The proof is in the new “About Last Night,” a sweet, silly, semi-raunchy Valentine’s Day confection directed by Steve Pink (“Hot Tub Time Machine”).

docs.lead_paragraph: 9 P.M. (13) NATIONAL THEATER: 50 YEARS ON STAGE In 1963, the National Theater in London raised its curtain with Laurence Olivier as its first artistic director. Eight hundred productions later, the organization celebrated its 50th anniversary in November with an evening of live performances and archival footage, overseen by its current artistic director, Nicholas Hytner, and presented here by “Great Performances.” Highlights include excerpts from “Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead,” with Benedict Cumberbatch; “The History Boys,” with its playwright, Alan Bennett, and two of its original stars, James Corden and Dominic Cooper; “Mourning Becomes Electra,” with Helen Mirren and Tim Pigott-Smith; “Bedroom Farce,” with Penelope Wilton; Judi Dench, above, singing “Send In the Clowns” from “A Little Night Music”; and archival scenes from “Hay Fever,” with Maggie Smith, and “Richard III,” with Ian McKellen. Joan Plowright, married for nearly 30 years to Olivier, recreates her Saint Joan on the stage of the Old Vic, home of the original National Theater.

docs.lead_paragraph: SAN FRANCISCO — Late last year, a designer and a geographer who met at M.I.T. revealed that they’d spent much of 2013 mapping every single swimming pool in Los Angeles — 43,123 of them, to be exact. Their satellite photos documented all the little aquamarine ovals and rectangles in a huge 74-book project called “The Big Atlas of L.A. Pools.” Though the cultural conversation mostly revolved around how unsettlingly easy it was for them to locate and discover personal details relating to each pool’s owner — address, property value, even sex-offender status — I found myself fantasizing instead about disappearing, and using those pools to do it.

docs.lead_paragraph: When the artist Jen Miller first started hosting “Reverend Jen’s Anti-Slam” in the mid-’90s, 100 people on a given night might have experienced anything from a comedy act to a primal-scream interpretive dance. These days, at a smaller venue on the Lower East Side called Old Man Hustle, the pool of audience members and participants might be 30 (though many now know one another). Miller, who considers her open-mike nights “the last vestiges of bohemianism in downtown New York,” attributes the decline to gentrification and the Internet, where people can more easily get their fix of performance art by up-and-comers. “There isn’t the incentive that we had in the ’90s to get out the door and actually do something.” But for Daniel Gallant, director of the Nuyorican Poets Cafe, which introduced open mikes in 1973, social media has been a boon: “The performances generate more viral activity online,” he says. docs.lead_paragraph: The Doctor Will Thrill You Now: Like a lot of brand-name novelists, Robin Cook drops a new book every year or two — in Cook’s case, medical thrillers with punchy, ominous titles like “Outbreak,” “Terminal” or “Contagion” that invariably land on the list. His latest, “Cell” (new at No. 11), is his 28th hardcover best seller since “Coma” made his reputation in 1977. Cook started his career as a practicing doctor, but eventually devoted himself more and more to writing, where the malpractice premiums are presumably lower. From the start, he has applied himself studiously to his craft. “It’s easier to get a book published if it’s going to be a best seller,” he told an interviewer in 1977, “so I went back to some old New York Times best-seller lists and tried to find books that came from theretofore unknown writers, to try to determine what kind of book had the best chances of making the list. I found the mystery-thriller genre seemed to do this best.” If that approach seems more robotic than inspired, well, so can Cook’s prose — “Cell” may be the first thriller to open with an entire paragraph about insulin molecules. (“Rapidly infiltrating the veins, they rushed headlong into the heart, to be pumped out through the arteries.”) Then again, Cook doesn’t make great claims for himself as a writer. “I’m a storyteller,” he told the CBS reporter Don Dahler earlier this month. “I have never been tempted to wear a turtleneck — big turtleneck, white turtleneck. I don’t drink.”

docs.abstract: Two books examine the lives of outrageous female celebrities of the 1920s.
docs.snippet: Two books examine the lives of outrageous female celebrities of the 1920s.
docs.lead_paragraph: “I find life quite impossible,” wrote Nancy Cunard, the English heiress famous in the 1920s for her fashionable excess, “as I cannot enjoy a thing without carrying it to all the extremes and then nearly dying of the reaction.” She wasn’t the only one blowing past her limits during that risky era, but as Judith Mackrell puts it in “Flappers: Six Women of a Dangerous Generation,” she was an audacious female forerunner preceding a “collective surge in expectation.” Women on the verge demanded more from life than marriage and motherhood. Joining Cunard in her restless experimentation were the outrageous actress Tallulah Bankhead, the brazen aristocrat Diana Cooper, the electrifying jazz dancerJosephine Baker, the Polish-Russian painter Tamara de Lempicka and America’s über-flapper, Zelda Fitzgerald. They shared an edgy ambition and a taste for immoderation that led them crashing through the public psyche, sometimes brilliantly, sometimes not, but always on toward emancipation — or at least on to the next great party. As Mackrell demonstrates so elegantly, their collective defiance redefined the feminine possible.

headline.main: Women of a Certain Era

docs.abstract: A historian argues that America’s supposed racial problems are in fact caused by economic exploitation.
docs.snippet: A historian argues that America’s supposed racial problems are in fact caused by economic exploitation.
docs.lead_paragraph: Americans have struggled mightily since the nation’s birth to overcome racial prejudice. Recently, as symbolized by President Obama’s ascendancy and his message of racial reconciliation, we have basically succeeded and are now healing from our racial wounds. Or so the story goes. In “A Dreadful Deceit,” the distinguished historian Jacqueline Jones vehemently rejects this redemptive and self-congratulatory narrative. She believes that the country’s racial problems have little to do with racism and everything to do with economic exploitation. And, she claims, we have not even begun to come to terms with this.

docs.lead_paragraph: Look at the famous pictures of the Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. marching on Selma, Ala., in 1965. In one of them you’ll see a man in big glasses two people to King’s left who looks halfway between Leon Trotsky and Santa Claus. That’s Abraham Joshua Heschel. From his perch at the Jewish Theological Seminary of New York, the Warsaw-born rabbi cast a long shadow over American Jewry, especially its Conservative variant, during the quarter-­century after World War II. He also became a byword for American Jewish social-justice activism — most of all for the alliance between Jews and blacks.

docs.lead_paragraph: “Grasshopper Jungle” is two for one. On one level, it is a darkly comic story about the end of the world. The book’s narrator and protagonist — 16-year-old Austin Szerba, of the fictional town of Ealing, Iowa — accidentally unleashes an infestation of six-foot-tall praying mantises, products of a scientific experiment gone kookily awry. With exoskeletons “as tough as the exterior hull of an aircraft carrier” and razor-sharp barbs on their arms, the bugs are killing machines invulnerable to bullets, and they set about devouring humanity. The praying mantises are perpetually horny as well as ravenous, able to smell a mate four miles away, breeding ceaselessly while slaughtering everything in their path. The earth is consumed by implacable forces and mindless appetite.

docs.lead_paragraph: Futurism is a tricky subject for curators because of the movement’s ties to fascism. Museums tend to show pre-World War I works that exemplify “heroic Futurism,” the Boccioni sculptures and Balla paintings that glorify speed and dynamism, while ignoring the violence and nationalism of later Futurist art. But “Italian Futurism, 1909-1944: Reconstructing the Universe,” opening Friday at the Guggenheim Museum, surveys this thrilling but troubled period in Italian art from beginning to end.

docs.lead_paragraph: When Grace Aneiza Ali moved to New York in 2006 for graduate school, she found herself immersed in a contradiction. Mr. Nelsons, who will officially become the music director of the Boston Symphony Orchestra next season, will lead the Lucerne orchestra in Brahms programs on the festival’s first two nights, on Aug. 15 and 16. Michael Haefliger, the executive and artistic director of the Lucerne Festival, said in a statement that by performing works planned by Mr. Abaddo “the memory of the Lucerne Festival Orchestra’s founder remains alive in the festival’s artistic programming.” He will conduct the orchestra in Brahms in another pair pf concerts on Aug. 22 and 24.

docs.lead_paragraph: The Los Angeles-based singer-songwriter Lo-Fang — the nom de musique of 30-year-old Matthew Hemerlein — wrote and recorded much of his debut album, “Blue Film” (out Feb. 25, 4AD), while globetrotting with friends. “There’s definitely a traveling quality to the record,” says Hemerlein, who worked with the acclaimed producer François Tétaz (Gotye) to bring his electro-tinged, “left-of-center pop” songs to life. In an interview last month, the singer described a nomadic recording process that took him to London, Nashville, Maryland and Southeast Asia, among other locales — including one particularly unusual violin session in Cambodia. “My friend who I went to Asia with was like, ‘Dude, you need to be playing while you’re riding an elephant up a mountain,’ ” he recalls. So he did just that, much to the delight of onlookers, as the friend recorded the melody.

docs.abstract: In the spring 2014 women’s fashion issue, T looks at the way women really want to dress.
docs.snippet: In the spring 2014 women’s fashion issue, T looks at the way women really want to dress.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the spring 2014 women’s fashion issue, T looks at the way women really want to dress. Our cover subject is the cult fashion-designer Phoebe Philo, whose quiet, understated designs for Céline give new meaning to the term “power dressing” — and are coveted by some of the smartest, savviest women out there. In our Sign of the Times essay, Cathy Horyn examines the divide between what women actually want to wear — beautiful clothes that they feel good in — and the tricked-out, challenging get-ups that come down the runway. We also celebrate three women who insist on doing things their way: the designer Maria Cornejo, whose art-inspired designs stay true to her singular vision; the up-and-coming singer Kelela, who is finding her voice somewhere between electronic music and old-school R&B; and the Fiat heiress Ginevra Elkann, who juggles duties as a film producer, art museum boss and mother while building a legacy — and a home — that goes beyond her famous name. Additional highlights include a behind-the-scenes look at Matthew Barney’s epic new art film; a pair of New York icons, Elaine Stritch and Chloë Sevigny, tune in to the latest rap music; and five prominent novelists — Colson Whitehead, Douglas Coupland, Mona Simpson, Joyce Carol Oates and Roddy Doyle — invite us into the spaces where they created their latest works. See all stories from the issue >>

docs.abstract: Scientists did not find a Dunkin’ Donuts on Mars, but they did figure out where a rock that looks like a small jelly doughnut came from.
docs.snippet: Scientists did not find a Dunkin’ Donuts on Mars, but they did figure out where a rock that looks like a small jelly doughnut came from.
docs.lead_paragraph: Scientists did not find a Dunkin’ Donuts on Mars, but they did figure out where a rock that looks like a small jelly doughnut came from. Last month, the rock, about an inch and a half wide, showed up in one of the photographs taken by the NASA’s Opportunity rover. In addition to the unusual appearance, it had not been there when Opportunity photographed the same spot on the Martian landscape less than two weeks earlier. A new photograph shows an overturned rock with a similar dark red center and white surface about a yard away. The jelly doughnut piece, named Pinnacle Island, broke off and rolled downhill when the rover drove over it in early January, scientists working on the mission said Friday.

headline.main: No Evidence of Coffee Break on Mars

(CBS) 48 HOURS PRESENTS: THE WHOLE GRITTY CITY Wynton Marsalis hosts this documentary, in which the filmmakers Richard Barber and Andre Lambertson follow five students in New Orleans marching bands whose directors, while preparing them to perform in Mardi Gras parades, have also instilled survival lessons in a city with one of the highest murder rates in the country. The students have all lost someone close to them. “This is the street I don’t like, because it has guns,” says Jaron Williams, 11, not far from where his 19-year-old brother was shot to death. “I cried the whole day. I couldn’t get him out of my head.” Then Jaron, above, joined the Roots of Music, a free music education program for middle schoolers, and learned to play the trumpet, earning his way into the Marching Crusaders — and a parade. “I feel like I’m the best thing in the world and I can’t be stopped,” he says. It’s the power of the music, Wilbert Rawlins Jr., one of the featured band directors ,maintains. “I don’t care if you just had something very tragic that happened to you in your life,” he says. “Once that band gives you that downbeat, and that music is right, and it’s powerful — just for that brief two or three minutes, you forget everything, every problem you had. You have no cares in the world.”

headline.main: What’s On Saturday

docs.lead_paragraph: Following is an excerpt from a document provided by the former National Security Agency contractor Edward J. Snowden. It is from the February 2013 edition of a monthly bulletin of SUSLOC, the acronym for the N.S.A. office that handles liaisons with Australian intelligence. It describes how Australian intelligence conducted surveillance of trade talks between Indonesia and the United States and, in the process, monitored communications between Indonesian officials and an American law firm retained by Indonesia for help with the trade dispute. The Australians then sought legal guidance from the N.S.A. (The document refers to the D.S.D — the Defense Signals Directorate — the former name of Australia’s counterpart to the N.S.A. In May 2013, the agency was renamed the Australian Signals Directorate, or A.S.D.)

docs.abstract: “About Last Night” took in $30 million to be the top newcomer, while “The Lego Movie” reigned at No. 1.
docs.snippet: “About Last Night” took in $30 million to be the top newcomer, while “The Lego Movie” reigned at No. 1.
docs.lead_paragraph: Bookended by Valentine’s Day and President’s Day, the weekend was a strong one for Hollywood, despite a flatlining “Winter’s Tale” and worries that winter storms in parts of the United States would keep moviegoers on their sofas. Certifying itself as a full-blown phenomenon, “The Lego Movie” (Warner Brothers) will take in a projected $60 million between Friday and Monday, for a two-week domestic total of roughly $140 million. “About Last Night” (Sony), one of three 1980s-era remakes to arrive over the weekend, was expected to be the No. 1 newcomer by selling a strong $30.2 million in tickets. Co-starring the popular comedian Kevin Hart, “About Last Night” cost $13 million to make. Third-place “RoboCop” from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer and Sony was a disappointment considering that it had a production budget of at least $100 million; if analyst projections hold, the science-fiction remake will take in $25.1 million over the long weekend, for a total since opening on Wednesday of about $30 million. (A Sony spokeswoman noted that “RoboCop” is performing “very strongly” overseas, where it has taken in more than $70 million since opening earlier this month.) “The Monuments Men,” also from Sony, was expected to be a solid fourth, generating a projected $17.3 million, for a two-week total of about $46 million. Analysts estimated that Universal’s poorly reviewed remake of “Endless Love” would take in about $15.2 million, which is fine for a lightly marketed movie that cost about $20 million to make. But Akiva Goldsman’s “Winter’s Tale” (Warner) bombed badly, taking in a projected $8.5 million. Adapted from the 1983 magical realism novel, “Winter’s Tale” cost Warner and financing partner Village Roadshow at least $45 million to make.

headline.main: ‘Lego Movie’ Tops Box Office, With ‘About Last Night’ Strong Second
headline.print_headline: ‘Lego Movie’ Is on Top at Box Office

The pre-eminent event is the invitation-only Colonial Ball, hosted by the Society of Martha Washington, in which young women, most of them Mexican-American, make their debuts in elaborate colonial gowns — weighing as much as 100 pounds and costing up to $30,000 — representing figures from America’s revolutionary history. Their goal: to recreate a party hosted by Martha herself. In this “Independent Lens” documentary, the director Cristina Ibarra follows two of the debutantes — one from a prominent Laredo family, the other a newcomer from Mexico — as they prepare for this rite of passage. docs.abstract: Is it possible to increase your chances of winning a seemingly random card game?
docs.snippet: Is it possible to increase your chances of winning a seemingly random card game?
docs.lead_paragraph: This week’s challenge was suggested by Steve Humble (aka Dr Maths), a mathematics educator from Newcastle University. The game starts with a standard 52-card deck of playing cards, which includes, obviously, 26 red cards and 26 black cards. At the start of a game, each player announces, one player after the other, a three-color sequence she will be watching for as the deck of cards is dealt out card by card. Cards are then dealt, and when a player’s sequence appears in a series of three consecutive cards, all cards in play are removed from the game as a winning trick. This continues until the full pack of 52 cards is exhausted. At the end, the player with the most tricks is declared the winner.

headline.main: Humble-Nishiyama Randomness Game

docs.lead_paragraph: In time for the upcoming sesquicentennial marking the end of the Civil War, the New-York Historical Society is featuring the exhibition “Homefront & Battlefield: Quilts & Context in the Civil War.” Running April 4 through Aug. 24, the exhibition uses approximately 130 objects, including quilts, clothing and other artifacts, to explore the ways that textiles expressed the era’s politics and culture. docs.lead_paragraph: “I don’t know why I’m telling you this, but we have changed the makeup three times in the past hour,” the makeup artist Val Garland said backstage at Mary Katrantzou. Garland’s early tests had included stronger, darker eyes and lips in an attempt to go someplace different from Katrantzou’s typical fresh-faced runway look. But why do away with a great thing? The designer and Garland decided to stick with what Garland called “very Mary” makeup. “The Katrantzou woman is pure and statuesque,” Garland said. “What stands out ultimately is her skin.” To complement the architecture and craftsmanship of the new collection, which strayed from the designer’s famed and oft-imitated digital prints, Garland opted for a down-to-earth and dewy look created using MAC products. Models’ lips were matte and natural, cheekbones were dusted with pink blush and eyelids sported a faint wash of silver. “I haven’t picked up a tube of mascara yet in London,” Garland said.

docs.snippet: The novelist Neil Gaiman, who turned his novelette “The Truth Is a Cave in the Black Mountains” into a performance, is bringing the show to the United States.
docs.lead_paragraph: The novelist Neil Gaiman (“American Gods”; “The Graveyard Book”). who turned his novelette “The Truth Is a Cave in the Black Mountains” into a performance that is a synchronized mix of music, art and storytelling for audiences abroad, is bringing the show to the United States. At a performance on June 25 at the Warfield in San Francisco and one on June 27 at Carnegie Hall, Mr. Gaiman, above, will read his tale of crime and search for buried treasure, accompanied by a score written for the event from the FourPlay String Quartet, from Sydney, Australia. As Mr. Gaiman reads, the images from the story will be displayed on a screen behind him, courtesy of the artist Eddie Campbell. Mr. Campbell will also illustrate a hardcover edition of “The Truth Is a Cave in the Black Mountains” when the story is published in June by William Morrow. The story had been in an anthology, but the new edition draws on the art created for the live performances. The 90-minute multimedia event was commissioned by the Sydney Opera House for its Graphic Festival in 2010 and was performed a year later in Tasmania for Mona Foma, an arts festival. The show is scheduled to travel to the Barbican in London on July 4 and 5.

headline.main: Neil Gaiman to Perform ‘Black Mountains’ in U.S.

docs.abstract: Steven I. Levine, a historian of China who is retired from the University of Montana, explains his effort to encourage candid commemoration of the events that culminated in the 1989 crackdown.
docs.snippet: Steven I. Levine, a historian of China who is retired from the University of Montana, explains his effort to encourage candid commemoration of the events that culminated in the 1989 crackdown.
docs.lead_paragraph: This year will mark 25 years since the upheavals of 1989 in China, when student protests prompted by the death of Hu Yaobang — the relatively liberal Communist Party leader who was pressed into resigning in 1987 — grew into huge, passionate demonstrations in Beijing and other cities demanding clean government, democratic change and respect for human rights. The party patriarch Deng Xiaoping deemed the demonstrations, based in Tiananmen Square in Beijing, a grave threat to party power. He authorized martial law in urban Beijing, ousted Mr. Hu’s successor as party general secretary, the reform-minded Zhao Ziyang, and ordered the People’s Liberation Army to end the demonstrations. The crackdown culminated in troops taking Tiananmen Square in the early hours of June 4. Across Beijing, many hundreds of protesters and ordinary citizens caught in the wrong place died from military gunfire, and soldiers also died at the hands of incensed residents. The precise number of dead has been in dispute ever since 1989.

headline.main: Q.&A.: Steven I. Levine on the Tiananmen Initiative Project

docs.abstract: On a January trip to the Anchorage area, the author finds that coffee, beer and winter sports can inject some life into the season’s cold, dark days.
docs.snippet: On a January trip to the Anchorage area, the author finds that coffee, beer and winter sports can inject some life into the season’s cold, dark days.
docs.lead_paragraph: Alone on a ridge in the Chugach Mountains of southern Alaska, I struggled to see. The wind was blowing upslope from the south, pelting my face with snow. Around me, all was white — or purple, as after a few hours of trying to rise in the sky, the sun had given up, leaving me alone in the dark. There was no shelter from the cutting wind as trees didn’t even try to grow at this extreme elevation. I had already had an exhausting day of climbing and descending the ridges, and I wasn’t sure how much more I could handle. Far below, the sea ice boulders strewn across the low tide line of the Turnagain Arm pointed the way back toward Anchorage, and civilization. But right about then, I didn’t know what I was going to do.

headline.main: Finding 3 Ways to Enjoy Alaska’s Winter
headline.print_headline: Surviving Winter, With More Fun Than Sunlight

docs.lead_paragraph: The snow has finally tapered off in most places around the city, but the truth is the mere forecast of snow makes me anxious these days. In my column this week, I describe the way many suburban parents, including my husband and myself, have been struggling to cope with the slew of snow-related school closings. We have been trying to juggle work — conference calls, column writing — and caring for our antsy little ones. It is no easy task. We have had seven snow days so far this winter in Montclair, N.J., which is why I commended New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio for keeping city schools open during most of these storms, despite some complaints from parents.

docs.snippet: “Child’s Pose,” by Calin Peter Netzer, is a family drama set in the new Romania.
docs.lead_paragraph: All kinds of monstrous mothers rage and rail in the movies, including those who love too little or too much. In Douglas Sirk’s 1959 melodrama, “Imitation of Life,” Lana Turner plays one type, a selfish white woman who’s blissfully indifferent to her child’s needs. Yet the more disturbing mother is played by Juanita Moore as a black domestic who smothers her own daughter in so much goodness that it’s no surprise that the girl flees. At the end, the saint’s daughter throws herself on her mother’s coffin; it’s a wonder she doesn’t leap in front of a train. In “Child’s Pose,” a drama with a story as cold, merciless and inevitable as a tomb, escape proves every bit as futile.

docs.abstract: Experts concerned about the over-diagnosis of A.D.H.D. too often attack parents in their zeal for change.
docs.snippet: Experts concerned about the over-diagnosis of A.D.H.D. too often attack parents in their zeal for change.
docs.lead_paragraph: Not long ago, amid what felt like a rising tide of criticism of parents of children who were being medicated for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (A.D.H.D.), readers in this space complained, and I joined them. It’s offensive, we said, to accuse parents (and teachers, and doctors) of using drug treatment to get “off the hook” for more complex problems, or teaching children to “reach for a pill” instead of finding another way to cope with a problem. It’s also useless. If A.D.H.D. is being over-diagnosed or overmedicated, pointing fingers won’t help either children who do need treatment or those who need something else.

headline.main: Educating Doctors About A.D.H.D. Without Resorting to ‘Ritalin Wars’

docs.lead_paragraph: Last February, the German tenor Jonas Kaufmann had a triumph at the Metropolitan Opera when he performed the title role of Wagner’s “Parsifal” in the company’s very bleak but theatrically riveting new production. On Tuesday night, a year later, Mr. Kaufmann was back at the Met in the title role of Massenet’s “Werther” on the opening night of Richard Eyre’s new production. It was another success for Mr. Kaufmann, currently the most in-demand, versatile and exciting tenor in opera.

docs.lead_paragraph: Like the mountainous collection of trinkets scattered throughout Pookie Burch’s East Village apartment, Trademark, the new women’s wear line she started with her younger sister Louisa, is tempting to close-read. The collection’s influences — Donald Judd, Maine in the 1960s — are apparent but ineffable, abstracted to an obscure likability. The clothes are the product of two self-taught designers who embrace eclecticism without veering into quirk — and whose father just so happens to be the billionaire venture capitalist J. Christopher Burch.

docs.lead_paragraph: Not long ago, I spent a month with Aniza and Dinko Muskardin, residents of the Croatian island of Cres, enjoying their emphatic Balkan hospitality in exchange for a few weeks’ help around their farm. I was besotted by my elderly hosts. I helped Dinko cut oak and juniper, search the hills for lost sheep and bottle the evil-smelling yellow wine that he aged in a cracked, slimy barrel. I was so besotted, in fact, that I didn’t hesitate when my host said to me, with an ominous gleam in his eyes, that it was time to kill the year-old “pecorina.” (Dinko was old enough to remember the Mussolini era, and we spoke in a pidgin of Italian.)

docs.lead_paragraph: In 1990, just before Saddam Hussein began lobbing Scud missiles at Tel Aviv and Haifa, my father and I paid our first visit to Israel. The men in my family can be adventurous: Before he emigrated from the Soviet Union, my father had taken to marching outside Leningrad’s Grand Choral Synagogue chanting: “We! Are! Jews!” with a group of fellow believers, a beautiful and lunatic gesture under an increasingly anti-Semitic regime. Likewise, the looming threat of Iraqi Scuds made us giddy at the thought of floating in the Dead Sea hoisting copies of The International Herald Tribune with its daily war cries by Saddam’s ever-present little buddy, Foreign Minister Tariq Aziz.

It still even had these original plastic discs, like thin translucent washers, that fit between the window roller and the door panel to keep the upholstery from being indented or pinched. docs.lead_paragraph: Before the passengers turned on the driver and began plotting a mutiny, the ride was smooth. The bus rolled out of the station in São Paulo at about 4 o’clock on a Wednesday afternoon last July, and within an hour it had shaken free of the city’s clotted tunnels, jammed overpasses and coded graffiti. By 6, we were barreling straight into a lurid sunset that endowed everything with the candied luster of fresh paint. Green hills, silver ponds, golden palms. Two parrots soared in tandem over a sugar-cane field, inviting us to drift into a pastoral trance.

docs.snippet: Picking up and going, with only a phone to capture the journeys.
docs.lead_paragraph: I’ve been to 55 places in the past year. I pick a spot and some dates, and then whoever wants to come can come, even if I don’t know them that well. I look for naturally beautiful spots that I’ve never been to before. There was a phase last summer when it was only swimming holes in upstate New York. And then after that, I wanted to go only to places with the biggest, weirdest rocks. Two specific memories come to mind from the past year: one is sleeping on a boat deck with my brothers under what felt like the darkest sky with the brightest stars in the Andaman Sea off Myanmar. And the other is standing with friends at the throat of an eroded volcano in New Mexico called Shiprock, right as the sun was setting on one of the last days of the year. Both places were shockingly beautiful and isolated and contained only a handful of people I really love.

docs.abstract: The Salish Sea, a wood bathtub by Seth Rolland, looks like a boat and costs as much as a Honda.
docs.snippet: The Salish Sea, a wood bathtub by Seth Rolland, looks like a boat and costs as much as a Honda.
docs.lead_paragraph: It looks like a teak salad bowl and costs as much as a new Honda. The Salish Sea is a wood bathtub by Seth Rolland, a furniture maker in Washington State. “I live in Port Townsend, the wooden-boat-building capital of the West Coast,” he said. He started building boats, but switched to furniture because it offered more artistic license. “A table has to have a flat surface and be about 28 inches high,” he said. “After that, everything is open.” Making the tub, for a client in Tennessee, involved 200 pieces of sustainable sapele wood, glued with epoxy, hand sanded, then waterproofed by a local wood kayak maker with layers of epoxy over an invisible fiberglass lining, on top of which went six coats of varnish. Shown above, it is 85 inches long and 36 inches deep. Prices start at $28,000. Information: sethrolland.com or 360-379-0414.

docs.abstract: While Studio 54 dazzled New York in the late 1970s, Tod Papageorge braved the miasma of pleasure-seeking to make clear pictures that had an authority to match his bulky camera.
docs.snippet: While Studio 54 dazzled New York in the late 1970s, Tod Papageorge braved the miasma of pleasure-seeking to make clear pictures that had an authority to match his bulky camera.
docs.lead_paragraph: A paradox of Studio 54 was that it was both the most exclusive party in town, stopping all but the chosen few at its impenetrable velvet rope, and the most accessible, bombarding the public with images of the glitterati and the high life inside. The club was a fantasy about which it was not necessary to fantasize, since torrents of ink and celebrity photographs did the work for you. If you wanted to know what it was like to rub shoulders (or more) with Halston or Liza or Name-Your-Boldface-Name, you could pick up a magazine that chronicled the rubbing. It was not just a place to see and be seen. In the miasma of sex and fame and money and pleasure that swirled around New York in the late 1970s, it was a place to be photographed, mass-produced and consumed as a shimmering commodity.

headline.main: This Ain’t No Disco. It’s a Photograph.

James Henry Gooding reported to the readers of his hometown newspaper on Feb. 8, 1864, “but with no knowledge of our destination.” His regiment, the 54th Massachusetts, the first regiment of African-American troops recruited from the Northern states, had won fame six months earlier when they attacked Fort Wagner on the South Carolina coast. Since then, they had been involved in mundane siege operations around Charleston, and morale was sinking. However, now that they were aboard steamers heading south, Gooding noted, “the excitement on board” was “intense.”

docs.lead_paragraph: I went to El Barrio this week thinking of Frank Espada. On blocks where renovated tenements stood alongside luxury high-rises, I strained to imagine what he had witnessed more than a half-century earlier, before anyone thought this stretch of Manhattan would sit in the cross hairs of gentrification. docs.snippet: Museums and music, cocktails and cuisine, history and Hudson River views are all part of a weekend in this richly textured part of the city.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the 18th century, the northern half of Manhattan Island served as a bucolic escape for New Yorkers with the cash to afford it and the horse and carriage to get them there. It’s easier to visit these days (the A train to Harlem being the most famous of many routes) and easier to get around, with the city’s newfangled green cabs in abundance in neighborhoods where yellow cabs have always been scarce. There’s also a whole lot more to do these days. Harlem, the Dutch settlement that became the black capital of America, is in the throes of gentrification: a mix of old and new, from gospel-filled black church services to fine cocktail bars abuzz with young professionals of all races. Meanwhile, farther north, between the island’s oldest surviving house and its largest swath of never developed land, is a Latino neighborhood the likes of which you can no longer find south of Central Park.

I would have traded her moving but relatively conventional 2009 novel, “A Gate at the Stairs,” for a horse-choking stack of 15 long, dense stories, each with the specific gravity (and the desperate levity) of “People Like That Are the Only People Here,” the astonishing centerpiece of her previous collection, “Birds of America.” But I was wrong! (Moore is one of the all-time great deployers of the exclamation point, that cheap and skinny punctuational powerhouse — she’s also a great deployer of the epithet — so I thought I’d try one and see how it felt. docs.lead_paragraph: Gregory Feifer’s “Russians: The People Behind the Power” joins a list of classic books by Western correspondents who have covered the politics and culture of what was once the Soviet Union. ­Hedrick Smith, Robert G. Kaiser, David K. Shipler and David Remnick, among others, wrote acclaimed accounts of what they witnessed as the Soviet Union first challenged the West and then gradually collapsed under the weight of a sclerotic regime. In August 1991, Feifer was an undergraduate spending a summer in Moscow when a group of hard-line Communist officials tried to carry out a coup in a last-ditch effort to prolong Soviet rule. Their failure only sped up the process of dissolution and led to an initial period of such euphoria that many people inside and outside the country believed — as did Feifer himself — that “the U.S.S.R. would be a part of the international community, enjoying the West’s previously unimaginable freedom and prosperity.”

docs.lead_paragraph: FKA Twigs is a mixed-race, tawny-skinned 26-year-old singer and dancer from rural Gloucestershire, England; her real name is Tahlia Barnett, and her old nickname was Twigs, hence “Formerly Known as Twigs.” Her music, on two EPs released in the space of a little more than a year, is tremulous and slow and commanding, with eerie barren stretches. (The second EP was produced by Arca, who worked on Kanye West’s “Yeezus.”) The methodical, strangely placed stresses of the beats signify a lot: isolation, displacement, missed connections. Something of interest — a little burst of rhythm or a bending, decaying electronic tone — occurs in nearly every bar. There’s some deconstructed, first-generation drum-and-bass in there, and Portishead and mid-period Madonna, too; she seizes on and transforms some drowsy energies in early-’90s pop.

Consider amontillado in a classic style, not sweetened, and go from there. During the tasting I wanted big sea scallops with a deep, almost candied burnish. That very evening, a memorable midcourse of sea scallops with pistachios and licorice at Restaurant Daniel suggested the pairing may be worth a test run. Raj Vaidya, the sommelier, was on board at once, with glasses of good amontillado. Though pistachios are sweeter and more herbaceous than the toasty essence of hazelnut that wraps the sherry, they drove the dish in the right direction. The recipe is my interpretation.

headline.main: A Scallop for a Sherry

docs.snippet: “In Secret” is the latest adaptation of Émile Zola’s “Thérèse Raquin.”
docs.lead_paragraph: “In Secret,” the latest adaptation of Émile Zola’s “Thérèse Raquin,” opens with a dip in the water and quickly comes ashore with furiously galloping horses and sweeping camera movements. The galloping suggests urgency; the camera movements imply narrative grandeur, or maybe directorial ambition. The darkly muted colors, evoking gathering storms and winter chill, add a brooding note. The river that runs alongside the road like a parallel boulevard will probably mean something only to those who have read Zola’s book, a classic of literary naturalism, which was published in 1867 and greeted by one appalled critic as “a pool of mud and blood.”

docs.lead_paragraph: You have to hate or fear something a lot to do what China did to Tibetan Buddhism. In the early 20th century, Tibet had thousands of active monasteries; when the Cultural Revolution ended in 1976, it had fewer than 10. The politics of blame are always tricky; some scholars argue that Tibetans themselves, for complicated reasons, contributed to the purge. But one reality is plain: By the time the mass demolition wound down, centuries’ worth of religious art was gone.

docs.lead_paragraph: Was any avowedly modern art movement as obnoxious and noisily contradictory as Italian Futurism? By turn aesthetically revolutionary and politically reactionary, farsighted and visually challenged, not to mention officially misogynist, it is both a stain on the Modernist brand and a point of pride. It needs all the help it can get and it receives a large dose from “Italian Futurism, 1909-1944: Reconstructing the Universe,” an epic exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum.

docs.lead_paragraph: In the new movie “3 Days to Kill,” Paris is full of thugs for hire with bald heads and dark suits, and the last thing they want to see — in many cases the last thing they do see — is Kevin Costner, unshaven and in faded jeans, shuffling down the hallway in their direction. Sometimes these tough guys make fun of the fact that Mr. Costner’s character, Ethan Renner, is American, calling him “cowboy” and other hilarious names. The deeper joke, perhaps unintentional, is that Ethan looks more French than most of the Parisians he encounters. With his loosely tied scarf and graying stubble, his sunglasses and his world-weary demeanor, he could easily pass for a philosophy professor or the leader of a Serge Gainsbourg tribute band. docs.abstract: The flu is hitting young and middle-aged people particularly hard this season, as a tough flu strain re-emerged and too few people were vaccinated, health authorities said Thursday.

docs.lead_paragraph: The flu is hitting young and middle-aged people particularly hard this season, as a tough flu strain re-emerged and too few people were vaccinated, health authorities said on Thursday. More than 60 percent of the severe flu cases in the United States this season have been in people 18 to 64 years old — about double the usual rate, they said. Typically, people at risk for flu complications include pregnant women, the elderly, children and people with compromised immune systems. The main flu circulating this season is H1N1, the “swine flu” that caused a pandemic four years ago. Dr. Thomas R. Frieden, chief of the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said that only a third of people ages 18 to 64 were vaccinated as of November, compared with nearly two-thirds of children and elderly people.

docs.lead_paragraph: Seven mortar shells fell on the Shiite town of Musayyib, south of Baghdad, on Thursday, killing 21 people and wounding 65, Iraqi officials said. Security officials said the shells had been fired from a Sunni area near Musayyib where security forces were conducting a weeklong search for fighters from the militant group the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria. No group immediately claimed responsibility for Thursday’s attack on the residential area. The Sunni area, Jurf al-Sakhar, was one of Al Qaeda’s strongholds during some of the worst of the sectarian fighting in 2006 and 2007. Now members of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria have moved to the area, according to officials, prompting the sweeps.

docs.lead_paragraph: TECH’S NEW FEEDING FRENZY  |  As soon as Facebook announced on Wednesday that it would acquire WhatsApp, a text messaging start-up, for up to $19 billion, almost everyone asked the same question: Why? What it boils down to is Facebook’s fear of missing out (F.O.M.O., for you cool kids). “Today, with Google, Facebook and others all fighting for the same customers and wallets, the competition has never been more intense, and big companies have never had to act so quickly — and with such conviction — to avoid being left behind,” David Gelles writes in DealBook. But the deal has raised fears that, by valuing the number of users above revenue, Facebook is inflating another dot-com bubble.

According to its website, the Cedarville Rancheria is a small, federally recognized tribe of 35 members on 26 acres in Cedarville, about 20 minutes from Alturas.

docs.abstract: The many lives of the early-20th-century cultural impresario Carl Van Vechten.
docs.snippet: The many lives of the early-20th-century cultural impresario Carl Van Vechten.
docs.lead_paragraph: One of the milestones of modernism occurred in Paris on May 29, 1913, when “The Rite of Spring” debuted at the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées and almost caused a riot. Startled by Stravinsky’s pounding rhythms and Nijinsky’s salacious choreography, the well-heeled philistines in the audience roared with disapproval while the connoisseurs, the happy few, tried shouting them down. One of the most memorable accounts of that first night was written by the American critic Carl Van Vechten, who allied himself decidedly with the latter camp, reporting that a kindred soul in the seat behind him was so carried away that he began beating a tattoo on the critic’s head with his fists. “My emotion was so great,” Van Vechten wrote, “that I did not feel the blows for some time.” Sharing his box was another pillar of the avant-garde, Gertrude Stein, who remembered certain details differently — as well she should, Van Vechten assured her. They had actually attended the less eventful second night of the ballet, but, as he suavely added, “one must only be accurate about such details in a work of fiction.”

docs.lead_paragraph: In Jay Cantor’s 1988 novel, “Krazy Kat,” the feline heroine praises Rube Goldberg contraptions: “Krazy liked having her mind pulled through one of Goldberg’s gadgets. He was a real artist; he had a vision.” Cantor’s vision often fo­cuses on public figures: George Herriman’s cartoon cat and J. Robert Oppenheimer; Che Guevara in Cantor’s first novel, “The Death of Che Guevara”; and now Kafka in “Forgiving the Angel.” These works and his graphic novel, “Aaron and Ahmed,” are contraptions of mixed materials: animal and human characters in “Krazy Kat,” fact and invention in “Che Guevara,” lucid writing and hallucinatory illustrations (by James Romberger) in “Aaron and Ahmed,” and now a story putatively by Kafka and stories about contemporaries who loved him. All of Cantor’s fiction (including “Great Neck,” his un-­gadgety novel of the American 1960s and ’70s) pulls the reader’s mind through sensitive history: atom bomb tests at Alamogordo; the Cuban revolution; the events of 9/11; and, in “Forgiving the Angel,” Stalin’s gulag and Hitler’s death camps.

docs.abstract: The proposed Bedford Historic District in Bed-Stuy is dividing residents. It all boils down to whether you think designation helps or hurts a community.
docs.snippet: The proposed Bedford Historic District in Bed-Stuy is dividing residents. It all boils down to whether you think designation helps or hurts a community.
docs.lead_paragraph: Most people would agree that the brownstones and small apartment buildings nestled in the southwest corner of Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, are for the most part drop-dead gorgeous. The 800 largely intact residential buildings, representing Italianate, Queen Anne, Romanesque Revival and Renaissance Revival styles, are executed in rich rusts, browns and terra cottas, and adorned with gracious bowed windows, generously proportioned stoops and adorable little turrets. The result, in the opinion of the New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission, is “an extraordinary well-preserved late-19th-century streetscape.”

headline.main: Argument Over a Brownstone Neighborhood

docs.abstract: The Swedish-African songstress and late-’80s style icon returns with a soulful, genre-blending new album.
docs.snippet: The Swedish-African songstress and late-’80s style icon returns with a soulful, genre-blending new album.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s been 18 years since Neneh Cherry released her last solo album. During that time, she’s been highly productive: she’s worked as a D.J. around Europe; formed a band, cirKus, with her husband and daughter; had guest spots on countless other records; co-hosted a cooking series on BBC Two and focused on raising her three children. It was the pain of loss, however, that brought her back to the spotlight. When her mother, the Swedish painter and textile artist Monica Karlsson (known as Moki), passed away in 2009, Cherry began to write in a journal, documenting dark emotional recesses she hadn’t previously explored. Her entries became the basis for “The Blank Project,” a soulful new album that’s danceable, but comes from the deep.

headline.main: Listen Up | Neneh Cherry Makes a Cathartic Comeback
headline.print_headline: Listen Up: Depth of Soul

docs.abstract: To complement the McDonald’s and SpongeBob SquarePants references on the runway, the house stuck to a simple, down-to-earth look for hair (and makeup).
docs.snippet: To complement the McDonald’s and SpongeBob SquarePants references on the runway, the house stuck to a simple, down-to-earth look for hair (and makeup).
docs.lead_paragraph: Despite the loud pop-culture references in Jeremy Scott’s first Moschino collection — strewn with McDonald’s, SpongeBob SquarePants and candy bar insignia — hair and makeup felt fairly down-to-earth. Backstage at yesterday’s show, the makeup artist Lucia Pieroni explained the inspiration for the “gorgeous, tomboyish” look. “It’s a Linda Evangelista kind, with very boyish eyebrows, brushed up to make them strong,” she said, adding that the flawless finish on the skin was inspired by Peter Lindbergh’s photography. To achieve the milky complexions, Pieroni stuck to the basics: a light foundation base, cream color on the eyes for a bit of shine and nude M.A.C. lipsticks that ranged from peachy and pink to soft shades of mocha. And on top of all those neutral faces, Paul Hanlon’s shaggy, pixie-cut wigs lent just enough attitude to the models as they walked past the front row, from which a very happy Katy Perry cheered them along.

headline.main: Backstage Beauty Report | Moschino’s Tomboy Tresses

So we had to make the girls look so beautiful.” To achieve that aim, Pecheux kept things simple. He left skin almost nude, with only a light application of M.A.C foundation — no blush or highlighter necessary. He didn’t touch the eyebrows or eyelashes either; the sole element of visible makeup was a simple sweep of M.A.C black eyeliner around the inner rims of the eyes and in the tiny spaces between eyelashes.

docs.abstract: Futuristic brushes from M.A.C took center stage backstage during New York fashion week.
docs.snippet: Futuristic brushes from M.A.C took center stage backstage during New York fashion week.
docs.lead_paragraph: Backstage at Diane von Furstenberg’s fall show, there was an unusual makeup tool being swept across the preternaturally smooth complexion of the singer Annie Clark, a.k.a. St. Vincent. From a distance, it looked a bit like a toothbrush or perhaps one of those hand-held, skin-firming wands. Nope! Turns out, it was one of three new Masterclass Makeup Brushes from M.A.C. Launched this winter, these newfangled tools perform all the usual beauty tasks — blending eye shadow, smudging eyeliner, buffing foundation into the skin, saturating the lips with color — albeit with a supercool design unlike that of a traditional brush. The most noticeable difference: The head and handle point toward the face, rather than away from it, which allows you to actually see what you’re doing in the mirror without hands getting in the way (imagine that!). Another plus: The densely packed synthetic bristles — or, rather, “cosmefibres” — evenly disperse makeup particles over the face, sans streaks. Oh, and the rubberized handles are just comfy to hold, which is key for a busy makeup artist like Regan Rabanal, who spent hours painting faces at numerous New York Fashion Week shows, including Zac Posen, Cushnie Et Ochs and Badgley Mischka.

headline.main: Brushing Up On the Most Curious New Beauty Tools

docs.lead_paragraph: MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif. — LAST June, in an interview with Adam Bryant of The Times, Laszlo Bock, the senior vice president of people operations for Google — i.e., the guy in charge of hiring for one of the world’s most successful companies — noted that Google had determined that “G.P.A.’s are worthless as a criteria for hiring, and test scores are worthless. ... We found that they don’t predict anything.” He also noted that the “proportion of people without any college education at Google has increased over time” — now as high as 14 percent on some teams. At a time when many people are asking, “How’s my kid gonna get a job?” I thought it would be useful to visit Google and hear how Bock would answer.

docs.lead_paragraph: My Sunday column, about the importance of anti-poverty efforts that focus on children, was motivated by a sense of frustration about the debate in this country. On the one hand, it’s terrific that we’re beginning to have a serious discussion about inequality, poverty and opportunity. On the other, the debate is mostly about the minimum wage and unemployment benefits, which to my thinking are useful but not the most cost-effective measures. The single most important measures we could take to build opportunity is to invest in children at the dawn of life to try harder to snap the cycle of poverty.

headline.main: Investing in Kids

docs.abstract: NBC announced it would resurrect the onetime hit science-fiction series as “Heroes Reborn,” a 13-episode series in 2015.
docs.snippet: NBC announced it would resurrect the onetime hit science-fiction series as “Heroes Reborn,” a 13-episode series in 2015.
docs.lead_paragraph: They’re coming back: once-dead television series, that is — revived as so-called event series by networks discovering a form that has distinguished cable drama for much of the past decade. The latest example is the onetime hit science-fiction series “Heroes,” which NBC announced it would resurrect as “Heroes Reborn,” a 13-episode series in 2015. The network used its platform of the Winter Olympics to tease out the announcement on Saturday, running a brief promotion. The news release that followed on Saturday night confirmed a few details: Tim Kring, who created the original “Heroes” in the 2006 television season, will be back as the executive producer. Before that, NBC is to create a digital series that will introduce the new story and characters. (Some original cast members may return.) Jennifer Salke, NBC’s president for entertainment, said in a statement that most details about the new version would be “appropriately shrouded in mystery.” Exactly when the show might appear is not known. Perhaps NBC will wait to see how the most immediate progenitor of the idea, Fox’s revival of “24,” fares this summer. CBS fashioned a hit last summer out of “Under the Dome” and has another such event-style short-run sci-fi series, “Extant,” with Halle Berry, planned for this summer.

headline.main: NBC to Bring Back ‘Heroes’ in New Form
headline.print_headline: NBC to Bring Back ‘Heroes’ in New Form

docs.lead_paragraph: Cabbies and limo drivers have so much to think about. Should they ally themselves with Uber or Lyft or Sidecar or someone else promising to revolutionize ground transportation? If they do, will they be insured if they get in an accident while working with their own car? And what of the future? Will they be replaced by a fleet of driverless cars, a technology that has been talked about so much it seems just around the corner?

docs.abstract: At Long Island City’s Chocolate Factory, an experimental theater group reworks the classic play into performance art, to sometimes bewildering effect.
docs.snippet: At Long Island City’s Chocolate Factory, an experimental theater group reworks the classic play into performance art, to sometimes bewildering effect.
docs.lead_paragraph: “This Was the End,” an experimental meditation on Chekhov’s “Uncle Vanya” at the supercool Long Island City arts space The Chocolate Factory Theater through March 8, begins both mesmerizingly and gratingly. Actors walk and run in and out of the set — a wall of doors of various shapes and sizes, sliding open and closed — while, ingeniously, the same actors do a version of the very same thing in a film projected imperfectly onto it. It’s an eye-popping sight. Meanwhile, a soundscape, chopped up from the Beatles’ “White Album,” assaults you, from speakers fitted close to the audience, half of whom covered their ears. The overall effect is hypnotic and somewhat unbearable. To what end? Is this collage meant to unpack the existential tedium of “Vanya” itself — a play in which characters frustrate us and break our hearts with their doddering romantic and career obsessions and resentments, all the while knowing that nothing will change?

headline.main: After Hours | A Digital Deconstruction of Chekhov’s “Uncle Vanya”

docs.snippet: Plush statement outerwear is popping up in fall/winter collections so often, it’s bordering on wardrobe-staple status.
docs.lead_paragraph: Last season, Miuccia Prada presented furs printed with hibiscus flowers and the artistic renderings of ladies’ faces in a rainbow of bright colors. This season, the ripples of those statement pieces have hit designers’ collections like a tidal wave, making the multicolored fur coat a must-have item for fall 2014. Although it is a trend we have seen before — especially at Céline, where color-blocked fur has become a signature of sorts — the frequency with which we’re now seeing fur with a graphic quality is making what once seemed like a luxury item feel like a new wardrobe staple. We first saw a version in New York at Altuzarra, where the young designer dressed up a simple, dark fur coat with vibrant colors like Yves Klein blue and tangerine. Then at J. Mendel, the house run by a long line of furriers, bold colors and abstract, latticelike color-blocking offered a fresh and modern take on the brand’s signature material. Finally at Marni in Milan, vertical panels of cobalt, white and crimson made an oversize silhouette seem long and lean — and a fluffy, neutral-colored collar provided the ultimate luxurious top-off.

headline.main: Three’s a Trend | Color-Blocked Fur Coats

docs.abstract: Just what should be included in a consumer privacy bill of rights? We asked the experts.
docs.snippet: Just what should be included in a consumer privacy bill of rights? We asked the experts.
docs.lead_paragraph: We are fast approaching a privacy crisis in the United States. Google, Facebook and other big Internet companies collect information about us, which they deploy in the service of advertisers. Big data brokers, like Acxiom, have developed sophisticated tools that allow them to know almost as much about us as we know about ourselves; they then sell that data to all kinds of companies that want to learn everything from our habits to our health, from our sexual orientation to our finances. The digital age has made it easy to collect medical data, which is supposed to be protected under federal law. Huge data breaches at big retailers like Target have made it seem unsafe to use credit cards. And I haven’t even mentioned the Edward Snowden revelations about the massive data collection by the National Security Agency.

headline.main: ‘The Wild West of Privacy’

docs.abstract: Maybe the contrived (some might say insane) atmosphere of the parent-preschool interview was actually helping me to see my daughter as an individual — a useful exercise in “detachment” parenting.
docs.snippet: Maybe the contrived (some might say insane) atmosphere of the parent-preschool interview was actually helping me to see my daughter as an individual — a useful exercise in “detachment” parenting.
docs.lead_paragraph: We’d just completed the school tour, and, with six other parents, were being escorted into a boardroom. Jon and I had spent the morning asking endless questions. (Do the ages mix? How do you handle separation? Where’s the coffee? No Danish?) Finally, I thought, we could sit back and listen to the preschool’s spiel, doodling with their branded pads and pencils. But the director, sitting at the head of the long table like a C.E.O., began. “Let’s go around,” she said. “One by one, describe your child in one word. Then, explain why this school is a good fit.” My heart galloped. She was asking us to pitch our kids — in public? Though this environment was contrived (some might say insane), it brought up a question I’d been contemplating: What is the best way to talk about my child?

headline.main: The Preschool Parent Interview: An Elevator Pitch for My 2-Year-Old

docs.snippet: An edgy rock’n’roll hair style looked wet but wasn’t, so as not to ruin the furs on the runway.
docs.lead_paragraph: For the Cédric Charlier runway, the hairstylist Laurent Philippon created a look based on a severe part. Starting above the left eye, he divided the hair all the way back, in a perfect line, to the bottom of the neck — a style inspired by the coifs of film noir heroines and silent-movie stars. To the left of the divide, tousled locks were tucked behind the ear and draped naturally over the shoulder. And on the right, they were pushed forward over the ear for what Philippon described as a “rock ‘n’ roll twist.” “I loaded the hair with Bb.Gel from Bumble and Bumble,” he explained while combing the product through and then ruffling it with his fingers. To finish, he used Bumble and Bumble’s new City Swept spray, which provided “beautiful natural shine.” The texture of this look is in fact quite stiff, but it offers the illusion of soft, wet hair. “I would have left it wet,” Philippon noted, “but we had fur.”

docs.abstract: For the Democratic strategist shaped by six years in the Clinton White House and the outcome of Bush v. Gore, going too far is never far enough.
docs.snippet: For the Democratic strategist shaped by six years in the Clinton White House and the outcome of Bush v. Gore, going too far is never far enough.
docs.lead_paragraph: On a hot Sacramento morning, Chris Lehane burst into a conference room filled with trial lawyers, lobbyists and one aggrieved mother, and laid out his battle plan: How to force California to raise its 40-year-old ceiling on medical-malpractice awards. Lehane, who is 46, spent six years working in the Clinton White House, battling the ethical scandals that seemed to confront the administration every day — typically by discrediting the accuser or leaking a document to undercut an impending news story critical of the president or the first lady. Now Lehane uses similar strategies — opposition research, attention-grabbing antics, the crafty manipulation of old and new media — for groups like this one, the Consumer Attorneys of California. The campaign to raise the cap on damages for pain and suffering in medical malpractice suits, which was set at $250,000, might have been handled legislatively, but much high-impact law in California is made at the ballot box, in the form of well-publicized voter initiatives. Influencing voters with his own extreme brand of performance politics has become Lehane’s specialty.

headline.main: Chris Lehane Out-Washingtons Washington
headline.print_headline: ‘Everyone Has a Game Plan Until You Punch them in the Mouth’

docs.lead_paragraph: BITCOIN’S SILVER LINING  |  The apparent collapse of Mt. Gox, the most prominent Bitcoin exchange, late Monday night naturally stirred outrage and panic. After all, a document circulating widely in the Bitcoin world said the company had lost 744,000 Bitcoins — about 6 percent of Bitcoins in circulation — worth more than $300 million at current exchange rates. But Bitcoin’s latest troubles did little to shake the confidence of many, and indeed, the virtual currency’s stumble may provide just the spark it needs to become a more mature part of the financial system, Nathaniel Popper and Rachel Abrams write in DealBook.

headline.main: A Silver Lining in Bitcoin’s Stumble

docs.lead_paragraph: Since the late ’90s, Shirin Neshat has been lauded for photographs, films and videos that explore the lives of Iranian women. Her first video, “Turbulent” (1998), featured a face-off between a male and a female singer in Islamic Iran, while “Women Without Men,” her 2009 feature film, focuses on the problems experienced by four women during the 1953 coup that brought the last shah to power. More recently, her work has addressed other countries in the Arab Spring, as in “Our House Is on Fire” (at Chelsea’s Rauschenberg Project Space, closing March 1), a group of poignant portraits of ordinary men and women in Cairo, survivors of the Egyptian revolution. “I wanted to humanize the people we think of as the other,” Neshat says.

docs.lead_paragraph: A full 36 hours, 36 days, or even 36 weeks could be spent exploring the thousands of Buddhist temples, Shinto shrines, Zen gardens, palaces, pagodas, parks and walking paths in Kyoto, the former imperial capital of Japan. So it’s little surprise that the most common complaint about the enchanting city is that there are too many tourists, especially during the spring cherry-blossom season. To avoid crowds, consider seeking out local haunts in far-flung neighborhoods, all within reach thanks to an extensive public transport system. You’ll quickly discover that many of Kyoto’s most rewarding attractions can’t be found in any guidebook. At least not yet.

docs.lead_paragraph: When a collector makes a hefty profit in reselling a contemporary painting or sculpture, the artist rarely benefits. Hoping to change that, three lawmakers introduced legislation on Wednesday that would allow artists to share in those proceeds. The bill proposes that artists receive 5 percent of the price of art that is resold at public auction for more than $5,000. Named the American Royalties Too act (so as to have the catchy abbreviation A.R.T.), the bill is a revised version of legislation that Representative Jerrold Nadler of New York, the ranking Democrat on the Courts, Intellectual Property, and Internet subcommittee of the House Judiciary Committee, introduced in 2011.

headline.main: New Bill Proposes Auction Royalties for Artists

Over time he embraced 12-tone techniques, but, in his own distinctive way, retained crystalline Neo-Classical clarity and directness. A recent recording from the conductor Gil Rose and the Boston Modern Orchestra Project presents a diversity of Berger works ranging from “Words for Music, Perhaps” (songs on Yeats poems originally composed in 1940) to the intricately engrossing Diptych: Collage I and Collage II from the 1990s. Mr. Rose has long been a Berger champion. (Anthony Tommasini)

docs.abstract: Google Earth images are the foundation for a series of locally made carpets.
docs.snippet: Google Earth images are the foundation for a series of locally made carpets.
docs.lead_paragraph: Weaving together geology, anthropology and Google Earth imagery, the Dutch designer Roosmarijn Pallandt has developed a series of carpets called Consider This Landscape a Territory. She begins with a bird’s-eye photograph of a rug-making region like northern Portugal, Nepal or Japan, then spends months researching each culture and its traditional rug-making techniques. Finally, she converts the original aerial image into a carpet produced by local artisans from natural materials. For the Flora rug, for example, which will be exhibited at the International Furniture Fair in Milan in April, a half-dozen women in Portugal hand-knotted felted wool yarn, jute and eucalyptus. The Ice carpet was knotted by a Tibetan family using wool from sheep, yak and goats combined with silk. The rugs can be ordered through Ms. Pallandt’s studio, in collaboration with Casalis, a Belgian carpet company. Prices start at about $1,168 per square meter. Information: roosmarijnpallandt.com.

docs.abstract: With head-to-toe matching knits, designers prove that the coziest of clothes can also be chic.
docs.snippet: With head-to-toe matching knits, designers prove that the coziest of clothes can also be chic.
docs.lead_paragraph: With cozy head-to-toe knits, designers are fast turning hibernation into a dressing category of its own. In their fall/winter 2014 collections, they’re layering oversize, monochromatic, luxurious separates — sweaters, pants, skirts and tunic dresses — that cradle the body in coziness. The first sighting of the look was in New York at The Row, where the designers Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen redefined our understanding of comfortable luxury with overwhelmingly voluminous knits including a cowl-necked, bell-sleeved sweater paired with a matching skirt. The trend continued at Marc Jacobs, whose neutral collection was filled with plush, nubby matching separates like a ribbed, V-neck long sweater with coordinating leggings and scarf. And at Edun, a sporty ivory tank dress paired with slouchy trousers and sneakers in the same color looked like the ultimate weekend wardrobe. The trend has continued to unfold in London, Milan and, now, Paris. Come fall, accepting unannounced guests at home will have never looked better.

In a statement, the committee said that Mr. Navalny had violated the terms of a travel ban in a case pending against him by driving outside of Moscow and by defying police officers at a rally on Monday. Mr. Navalny has said that the case against him, in which he stands accused of stealing more than $800,000 from the Russian branch of Yves Rocher, is politically motivated. The Associated Press said he was accused of doing so by charging an excessive price for shipping services. Mr. Navalny came to prominence by publishing online his investigations into government corruption. If approved, house arrest, which in other cases has included a ban on Internet use, could effectively remove Mr. Navalny from public life.

docs.abstract: Bringing extinct animals back to life is really happening — and it’s going to be very, very cool. Unless it ends up being very, very bad.
docs.snippet: Bringing extinct animals back to life is really happening — and it’s going to be very, very cool. Unless it ends up being very, very bad.
docs.lead_paragraph: The first time Ben Novak saw a passenger pigeon, he fell to his knees and remained in that position, speechless, for 20 minutes. He was 16. At 13, Novak vowed to devote his life to resurrecting extinct animals. At 14, he saw a photograph of a passenger pigeon in an Audubon Society book and “fell in love.” But he didn’t know that the Science Museum of Minnesota, which he was then visiting with a summer program for North Dakotan high-school students, had them in their collection, so he was shocked when he came across a cabinet containing two stuffed pigeons, a male and a female, mounted in lifelike poses. He was overcome by awe, sadness and the birds’ physical beauty: their bright auburn breasts, slate-gray backs and the dusting of iridescence around their napes that, depending on the light and angle, appeared purple, fuchsia or green. Before his chaperones dragged him out of the room, Novak snapped a photograph with his disposable camera. The flash was too strong, however, and when the film was processed several weeks later, he was haunted to discover that the photograph hadn’t developed. It was blank, just a flash of white light.

headline.main: The Mammoth Cometh

docs.snippet: The Lunchbox,” by Ritesh Batra, puts Old Hollywood style in a Mumbai that has escaped the cyber world.
docs.lead_paragraph: “The Lunchbox,” Ritesh Batra’s debut feature, is a romance that takes place in Mumbai, but its style is more Hollywood than Bollywood, and Old Hollywood at that. Though Mr. Batra and his cinematographer, Michael Simmonds, shot the film on location in the bustling modern city, with a naturalism alien to both American studio-era back-lot fantasies and present-day Indian musical extravaganzas, “The Lunchbox” has the measured pace and Classical restraint of a romance from the ’30s or ’40s. The comedy is more wry than uproarious, the melodrama gently poignant rather than operatic, and the sentimentality just sweet enough to be satisfying rather than bothersome.

docs.snippet: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau accused an Indiana-based chain of practicing “predatory student lending.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Honest, well-run for-profit colleges can be helpful to students who do not qualify for traditional schools. But the robber barons in the for-profit sector represent a menace that requires more federal oversight. They saddle students with crushing debt while furnishing them useless degrees – or no degrees at all. These schools have been known to push students who are eligible for low-cost, federal loans into ruinously priced private loans that have fewer consumer protections and that give borrowers who get in trouble little choice but to default. That in turn makes it difficult for them to find jobs, get credit or rent apartments. And because private student loans are difficult to escape through bankruptcy, the stricken borrower might never recover.

headline.main: The Robber Barons of the For-Profit College Sector

docs.lead_paragraph: BEIJING — Is there a Chinese word for chutzpah? If there is, the Shanghai artist Xu Zhen, often called the Maurizio Cattelan of China, fits the bill. Combining the roles of artist, curator and chief executive of his own corporation, MadeIn, he has forged a career of pushing buttons, consistently riling audiences with shocking installations though rarely provoking the Chinese government. He is considered the leader of a younger generation of Chinese artists who have disengaged from the Mao-driven paintings of the 1990s in favor of more conceptual projects. Xu Zhen (pronounced shoo-jen) is also the commissioned artist for the sprawling 2014 Armory Show, which opens on Thursday on Piers 92 and 94 in Manhattan with a focus on China.
